entries.8c6ea8d1a9e12e2f1b0ca7f556750068da309191: <div sID="gen5785" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="1Sam.25" sID="1Sam.25"/> <div eID="gen5785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5786" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5787" type="x-p"/> We have here some intermission of David's troubles by Saul. Providence favoured him with a breathing time, and yet this chapter gives us instances of the troubles of David. If one vexation seems to be over, we must not be secure; a storm may arise from some other point, as here to David. I. Tidings of the death of Samuel could not but trouble him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">ver. 1</reference>. But, II. The abuse he received from Nabal is more largely recorded in this chapter. 1. The character of Nabal, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2-1Sam.25.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. 2. The humble request sent to him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.4-1Sam.25.9">ver. 4-9</reference>. 3. His churlish answer, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.10-1Sam.25.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. 4. David's angry resentment of it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.13">ver. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.21">21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.22">22</reference>. 5. Abigail's prudent care to prevent the mischief it was likely to bring upon her family, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.14-1Sam.25.20">ver. 14-20</reference>. 6. Her address to David to pacify him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.23-1Sam.25.31">ver. 23-31</reference>. 7. David's favourable reception of her, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.32-1Sam.25.35">ver. 32-35</reference>. 8. The death of Nabal, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36-1Sam.25.38">ver. 36-38</reference>. 9. Abigail's marriage to David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.39-1Sam.25.44">ver. 39-44</reference>. <div eID="gen5787" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5786" type="introduction"/>
entries.c4b0f24b12c050b41773953798a8a078e9bbacf7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13"/><title type="x-s3">The Death of Samuel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5788" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Samuel died; and all the Israelites were gathered together, and lamented him, and buried him in his house at Ramah. And David arose, and went down to the wilderness of Paran. <div eID="gen5788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5789" type="x-p"/> We have here a short account of Samuel's death and burial. 1. Though he was a great man, and one that was admirably well qualified for public service, yet he spent the latter end of his days in retirement and obscurity, not because he was superannuated (for he knew how to preside in a college of the prophets, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.20">ch. xix. 20</reference>), but because Israel had rejected him, for which God thus justly chastised them, and because his desire was to be quiet and to enjoy himself and his God in the exercises of devotion now in his advanced years, and in this desire God graciously indulged him. Let old people be willing to rest themselves, though it look like burying themselves alive. 2. Though he was a firm friend to David, for which Saul hated him, as also for dealing plainly with him, yet he died in peace even in the worst of the days of the tyranny of Saul, who, he sometimes feared, would kill him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.2">ch. xvi. 2</reference>. Though Saul loved him not, yet he feared him, as Herod did John, and feared the people, for all knew him to be a prophet. Thus is Saul restrained from hurting him. 3. All Israel lamented him; and they had reason, for they had all a loss in him. His personal merits commanded this honour to be done him at his death. His former services to the public, when he judged Israel, made this respect to his name and memory a just debt; it would have been very ungrateful to have withheld it. The sons of the prophets had lost the founder and president of their college, and whatever weakened them was a public loss. But that was not all: Samuel was a constant intercessor for Israel, prayed daily for them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.23">ch. xii. 23</reference>. If he go, they part with the best friend they have. The loss is the more grievous at this juncture when Saul has grown so outrageous and David is driven from his country; never more need of Samuel than now, yet now he is removed. We will hope that the Israelites lamented Samuel's death the more bitterly because they remembered against themselves their own sin and folly in rejecting him and desiring a king. Note, (1.) Those have hard hearts who can bury their faithful ministers with dry eyes, who are not sensible of the loss of those who have prayed for them and taught them the way of the Lord. (2.) When God's providence removes our relations and friends from us we ought to be humbled for our misconduct towards them while they were with us. 4. They buried him, not in the school of the prophets at Naioth, but in his own house (or perhaps in the garden pertaining to it) at Ramah, where he was born. 5. David, thereupon, went down to the wilderness of Paran, retiring perhaps to mourn the more solemnly for the death of Samuel. Or, rather, because now that he had lost so good a friend, who was (and he hoped would be) a great support to him, he apprehended his danger to be greater than ever, and therefore withdrew to a wilderness, out of the limits of the land of Israel; and now it was that he <hi type="italic">dwelt in the tents of Kedar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.120.5">Ps. cxx. 5</reference>. In some parts of this wilderness of Paran Israel wandered when they came out of Egypt. The place would bring to mind God's care concerning them, and David might improve that for his own encouragement, now in his wilderness-state. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13"/> <div eID="gen5789" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Sends to Nabal. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5790" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> And <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a man in Maon, whose possessions <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Carmel; and the man <hi type="italic">was</hi> very great, and he had three thousand sheep, and a thousand goats: and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now the name of the man <hi type="italic">was</hi> Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and <hi type="italic">she was</hi> a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man <hi type="italic">was</hi> churlish and evil in his doings; and he <hi type="italic">was</hi> of the house of Caleb. <hi type="super">4</hi> And David heard in the wilderness that Nabal did shear his sheep. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David sent out ten young men, and David said unto the young men, Get you up to Carmel, and go to Nabal, and greet him in my name: <hi type="super">6</hi> And thus shall ye say to him that liveth <hi type="italic">in prosperity,</hi> Peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> both to thee, and peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to thine house, and peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto all that thou hast. <hi type="super">7</hi> And now I have heard that thou hast shearers: now thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them, all the while they were in Carmel. <hi type="super">8</hi> Ask thy young men, and they will shew thee. Wherefore let the young men find favour in thine eyes: for we come in a good day: give, I pray thee, whatsoever cometh to thine hand unto thy servants, and to thy son David. <hi type="super">9</hi> And when David's young men came, they spake to Nabal according to all those words in the name of David, and ceased. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Nabal answered David's servants, and said, Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> David? and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master. <hi type="super">11</hi> Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto men, whom I know not whence they <hi type="italic">be?</hi> <div eID="gen5790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5791" type="x-p"/> Here begins the story of Nabal. <div eID="gen5791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5792" type="x-p"/> I. A short account of him, who and what he was (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2-1Sam.25.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), a man we should never have heard of if there had not happened some communication between him and David. Observe, 1. His name: <hi type="italic">Nabal—a fool;</hi> so it signifies. It was a wonder that his parents would give him that name and an ill omen of what proved to be this character. Yet indeed we all of us deserve to be so called when we come into the world, for <hi type="italic">man is born like the wild ass's colt</hi> and <hi type="italic">foolishness is bound up in our hearts.</hi> 2. His family: He was of the house of Caleb, but was indeed of another spirit. He inherited Caleb's estate; for Maon and Carmel lay near Hebron, which was given to Caleb (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.54-Josh.15.55">Josh. xv. 54, 55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.14.14">xiv. 14</reference>), but he was far from inheriting his virtues. He was a disgrace to his family, and then it was no honour to him. <hi type="italic">Degeneranti genus opprobrium—A Good extraction is a reproach to him who degenerates from it.</hi> The LXX., and some other ancient versions, read it appellatively, not, He was a Calebite, but He was a dogged man, of a currish disposition, surly and snappish, and always snarling. He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anthropos kynikos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a man that was a cynic.</hi> 3. His wealth: He was very great, that is, very rich (for riches make men look great in the eye of the world), otherwise, to one that takes his measures aright, he really looked very mean. Riches are common blessings, which God often gives to Nabals, to whom he gives neither wisdom nor grace. 4. His wife—Abigail, a woman of great understanding. Her name signifies, <hi type="italic">the joy of her father;</hi> yet he could not promise himself much joy of her when he married her to such a husband, enquiring more after his wealth than after his wisdom. Many a child is thrown away upon a great heap of the dirt of worldly wealth, married to that, and to nothing else that is desirable. Wisdom is good with an inheritance, but an inheritance is good for little without wisdom. Many an Abigail is tied to a Nabal; and if it be so, be her understanding, like Abigail's, ever so great, it will be little enough for her exercises. 5. His character. He had no sense either of honour or honesty; not of honour, for he was churlish, cross, and ill-humoured; not of honesty, for he was evil in his doings, hard and oppressive, and a man that cared not what fraud and violence he used in getting and saving, so he could but get and save. This is the character given of Nabal by him who knows what every man is. <div eID="gen5792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5793" type="x-p"/> II. David's humble request to him, that he would send him some victuals for himself and his men. <div eID="gen5793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5794" type="x-p"/> 1. David, it seems, was in such distress that he would be glad to be beholden to him, and did in effect come a begging to his door. What little reason have we to value the wealth of this world when so great a churl as Nabal abounds and so great a saint as David suffers want! Once before we had David begging his bread, but then it was of Ahimelech the high priest, to whom one would not grudge to stoop. But to send a begging to Nabal was what such a spirit as David had could not admit without some reluctancy; yet, if Providence bring him to these straits, he will not say that to beg he is ashamed. Yet see <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Ps. xxxvii. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen5794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5795" type="x-p"/> 2. He chose a good time to send to Nabal, when he had many hands employed about him in shearing his sheep, for whom he was to make a plentiful entertainment, so that good cheer was stirring. Had he sent at another time, Nabal would have pretended he had nothing to spare, but now he could not have that excuse. It was usual to make feasts at their sheep-shearings, as appears by Absalom's feast on that occasion (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.24">2 Sam. xiii. 24</reference>), for wool was one of the staple commodities of Canaan. <div eID="gen5795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5796" type="x-p"/> 3. David ordered his men to deliver their message to him with a great deal of courtesy and respect: "<hi type="italic">Go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.</hi> Tell him I sent you to present my service to him, and to enquire how he does and his family," <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.5">v. 5</reference>. He puts words in their mouths (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus shall you say to him that liveth;</hi> our translators add, <hi type="italic">in prosperity,</hi> as if those live indeed that live as Nabal did, with abundance of the wealth of this world about them; whereas, in truth, those that<hi type="italic">live in pleasure are dead while they live,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">1 Tim. v. 6</reference>. This was, methinks too high a compliment to pass upon Nabal, to call him <hi type="italic">the man that liveth.</hi> David knew better things, that in God's favour is life, not in the world's smiles; and by the rough answer he was well enough served, for this too smooth address to such a muck-worm. Yet his good wishes were very commendable. "<hi type="italic">Peace be to thee,</hi> all good both to soul and body. <hi type="italic">Peace be to thy house and to all that thou hast.</hi>" Tell him I am a hearty well-wisher to his health and prosperity. He bids them call him his <hi type="italic">son David</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.8">v. 8</reference>), intimating that, for his age and estate, David honoured him as a father, and therefore hoped to receive some fatherly kindness from him. <div eID="gen5796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5797" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleaded the kindness which Nabal's shepherds had received from David and his men; and one good turn requires another. He appeals to Nabal's own servants, and shows that when David's soldiers were quartered among Nabal's shepherds, (1.) They did not hurt them themselves, did them no injury, gave them no disturbance, were not a terror to them, nor took any of the lambs out of the flock. Yet, considering the character of David's men, men in distress, and debt, and discontented, and the scarcity of provisions in his camp, it was not without a great deal of care and good management that they were kept from plundering. (2.) They protected them from being hurt by others. David himself does but <hi type="italic">intimate</hi> this, for he would not boast of his good offices: <hi type="italic">Neither was there aught missing to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.7">v. 7</reference>. But Nabal's servants, to whom he appealed, went further (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">They were a wall unto us, both by night and day.</hi> David's soldiers were a guard to Nabal's shepherds when the bands of the <hi type="italic">Philistines robbed the threshing-floors</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1">ch. xxiii. 1</reference>) and would have robbed the sheep-folds. From those plunderers Nabal's flocks were protected by David's care, and therefore he says, <hi type="italic">Let us find favour in thy eyes.</hi> Those that have shown kindness may justly expect to receive kindness. <div eID="gen5797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5798" type="x-p"/> 5. He was very modest in his request. Though David was anointed king, he insisted not upon royal dainties, but, "Give whatsoever comes to thy hand, and we will be thankful for it." Beggars must not be choosers. Those that deserved to have been served first will now be glad of what is left. They plead, <hi type="italic">We come in a good day,</hi> a festival, when not only the provision is more plentiful, but the heart and hand are usually more open and free than at other times, when much may be spared and yet not be missed. David demands not what he wanted as a debt, either by way of tribute as he was a king, or by way of contribution as he was a general, but asks it as a boon to a friend, that was his humble servant. David's servants delivered their message faithfully and very handsomely, not doubting but to go back well laden with provisions. <div eID="gen5798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5799" type="x-p"/> III. Nabal's churlish answer to this modest petition, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.10-1Sam.25.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. One could not have imagined it possible that any man should be so very rude and ill-conditioned as Nabal was. David called himself his <hi type="italic">son,</hi> and asked bread and a fish, but, instead thereof, Nabal gave him a stone and a scorpion; not only denied him, but abused him. If he had not thought fit to send him any supplies for fear of Ahimelech's fate, who paid dearly for his kindness to David; yet he might have given a civil answer, and made the denial as modest as the request was. But, instead of that, he falls into a passion, as covetous men are apt to do when they are asked for any thing, thinking thus to cover one sin with another, and by abusing the poor to excuse themselves from relieving them. But God will not thus be mocked. 1. He speaks scornfully of David as an insignificant man, not worth taking notice of. The Philistines could say of him, <hi type="italic">This is</hi> David <hi type="italic">the king of the land,</hi> that <hi type="italic">slew his ten thousands</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11">ch. xxi. 11</reference>), yet Nabal his near neighbour, and one of the same tribe, affects not to know him, or not to know him to be a man of any merit or distinction: <hi type="italic">Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse?</hi> He could not be ignorant how much the country was obliged to David for his public services, but his narrow soul thinks not of paying any part of that debt, nor so much as of acknowledging it; he speaks of David as an inconsiderable man, obscure, and not to be regarded. Think it not strange if great men and great merits be thus disgraced. 2. He upbraids him with his present distress, and takes occasion from it to represent him as a bad man, that was fitter to be set in the stocks for a vagrant than to have any kindness shown him. How naturally does he speak the churlish clownish language of those that hate to give alms! <hi type="italic">There are many servants now-a-days</hi> (as if there had been none such in former days) <hi type="italic">that break every man from his master,</hi> suggesting that David was one of them himself ("He might have kept his place with his master Saul, and then he needed not have sent to me for provisions"), and also that he entertained and harboured those that were fugitives like himself. It would make one's blood rise to hear so great and good a man as David thus vilified and reproached by such a base churl as Nabal. <hi type="italic">But the vile person will speak villany,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5-Isa.32.7">Isa. xxxii. 5-7</reference>. If men bring themselves into straits by their own folly, yet they are to be pitied and helped, and not trampled upon and starved. But David was reduced to this distress, not by any fault, no, nor any indiscretion, of his own, but purely by the good services he had done to his country and the honours which his God had put upon him; and yet he was represented as a fugitive and runagate. Let this help us to bear such reproaches and misrepresentations of us with patience and cheerfulness, and make us easy under them, that it has often been the lot of the excellent ones of the earth. Some of the best men that ever the world was blest with were counted as the <hi type="italic">off-scouring of all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.13">1 Cor. iv. 13</reference>. 3. He insists much upon the property he had in the provisions of his table, and will by no means admit any body to share in them. "It is my bread and my flesh, yes, and my water too (though <hi type="italic">usus communis aquarum</hi>—<hi type="italic">water is every one's property</hi>), and it is prepared for my shearers," priding himself in it that it was all his own; and who denied it? Who offered to dispute his title? But this, he thinks, will justify him in keeping it all to himself, and giving David none; for may he not do what he will with his own? Whereas we mistake if we think we are absolute lords of what we have and may do what we please with it. No, we are but stewards, and must use it as we are directed, remembering it is not our own, but his that entrusted us with it. Riches are <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta allotria</hi></hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.12">Luke xvi. 12</reference>); they are <hi type="italic">another's,</hi> and we ought not to talk too much of their being our own.
entries.399ccacfb4831618ae37e7e91d81606dec972432: <div eID="gen5799" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abigail Wise Resolution. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5800" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> So David's young men turned their way, and went again, and came and told him all those sayings. <hi type="super">13</hi> And David said unto his men, Gird ye on every man his sword. And they girded on every man his sword; and David also girded on his sword: and there went up after David about four hundred men; and two hundred abode by the stuff. <hi type="super">14</hi> But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, saying, Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master; and he railed on them. <hi type="super">15</hi> But the men <hi type="italic">were</hi> very good unto us, and we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing, as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields: <hi type="super">16</hi> They were a wall unto us both by night and day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep. <hi type="super">17</hi> Now therefore know and consider what thou wilt do; for evil is determined against our master, and against all his household: for he <hi type="italic">is such</hi> a son of Belial, that <hi type="italic">a man</hi> cannot speak to him. <div eID="gen5800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5801" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The report made to David of the abuse Nabal had given to his messengers (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">They turned their way.</hi> They showed their displeasure, as became them to do, by breaking off abruptly from such a churl, but prudently governed themselves so well as not to render railing for railing, not to call him as he deserved, much less to take by force what ought of right to have been given them, but came and told David that he might do as he thought fit. Christ's servants, when they are thus abused, must leave it to him to plead his own cause and wait till he appear in it. The servant showed his lord what affronts he had received, but did not return them, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.21">Luke xiv. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen5801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5802" type="x-p"/> II. David's hasty resolution hereupon. He girded on his sword, and ordered his men to do so too, to the number of 400, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.13">v. 13</reference>. And what he said we are told, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.21-1Sam.25.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. 1. He repented of the kindness he had done to Nabal, and looked upon it as thrown away upon him. He said, "<hi type="italic">surely in vain have I kept all that this fellow hath in the wilderness.</hi> I thought to oblige him and make him my friend, but I see it is to no purpose. He has no sense of gratitude, nor is he capable of receiving the impressions of a good turn, else he could not have used me thus. He hath <hi type="italic">requited me evil for good.</hi>" But, when we are thus requited, we should not repent of the good we have done, nor be backward to do good another time. God is kind to the evil and unthankful, and why may not we? 2. He determined to destroy Nabal and all that belonged to him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.22">v. 22</reference>. Here David did not act like himself. His resolution was bloody, to cut off all the males of Nabal's house, and spare none, man nor man-child. The ratification of his resolution was passionate: <hi type="italic">So, and more also do to God</hi> (he was going to say <hi type="italic">to me,</hi> but that would better become Saul's mouth, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.44">ch. xiv. 44</reference>, than David's, and therefore he decently turns it off) <hi type="italic">to the enemies of David. Is this thy voice, O David?</hi> Can the man after God's own heart speak thus unadvisedly with his lips? Has he been so long in the school of affliction, where he should have learned patience, and yet so passionate? Is this he who used to be dumb and deaf when he was reproached (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>), who but the other day spared him who sought his life, and yet now will not spare any thing that belongs to him who has only put an affront upon his messengers? He who at other times used to be calm and considerate is now put into such a heat by a few hard words that nothing will atone for them but the blood of a whole family. Lord, what is man! What are the best of men, when God leaves them to themselves, to try them, that they may know what is in their hearts? From Saul David expected injuries, and against those he was prepared and stood upon his guard, and so kept his temper; but from Nabal he expected kindness, and therefore the affront he gave him was a surprise to him, found him off his guard, and, by a sudden and unexpected attack, put him for the present into disorder. What need have we to pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation!</hi> <div eID="gen5802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5803" type="x-p"/> III. The account given of this matter to Abigail by one of the servants, who was more considerate than the rest, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.14">v. 14</reference>. Had this servant spoken to Nabal, and shown him the danger he had exposed himself to by his own rudeness, he would have said, "Servants are now-a-days so saucy, and so apt to prescribe, that there is no enduring them," and, it may be, would have turned him out of doors. But Abigail, being a woman of good understanding, took cognizance of the matter, even from her servant, who, 1. Did David justice in commending him and his men for their civility to Nabal's shepherds, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.15-1Sam.25.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. "The men were very good to us, and, though they were themselves exposed, yet they protected us and were a wall unto us." Those who do that which is good shall, one way or other, have the praise of the same. Nabal's own servant will be a witness for David that he is a man of honour and conscience, whatever Nabal himself says of him. And, 2. He did Nabal no wrong in condemning him for his rudeness to David's messengers: <hi type="italic">He railed on them</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">he flew upon them</hi> (so the word is) with an intolerable rage; "for," say they, "it is his usual practice, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.17">v. 17</reference>. He is such a son of Belial, so very morose and intractable, that a man cannot speak to him but he flies into a passion immediately." Abigail knew it too well herself. 3. He did Abigail and the whole family a kindness in making her sensible what was likely to be the consequence. He knew David so well that he had reason to think he would highly resent the affront, and perhaps had had information of David's orders to his men to march that way; for he is very positive <hi type="italic">evil is determined against our master, and all his household,</hi> himself among the rest, would be involved in it. Therefore he desires his mistress to consider what was to be done for their common safety. They could not resist the force David would bring down upon them, nor had they time to send to Saul to protect them; something therefore must be done to pacify David.
entries.4796ff7c58ea2f67252fd020a99d20d70fa10f12: <div eID="gen5803" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abigail Meets David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5804" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched <hi type="italic">corn,</hi> and a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid <hi type="italic">them</hi> on asses. <hi type="super">19</hi> And she said unto her servants, Go on before me; behold, I come after you. But she told not her husband Nabal. <hi type="super">20</hi> And it was <hi type="italic">so, as</hi> she rode on the ass, that she came down by the covert of the hill, and, behold, David and his men came down against her; and she met them. <hi type="super">21</hi> Now David had said, Surely in vain have I kept all that this <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> hath in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that <hi type="italic">pertained</hi> unto him: and he hath requited me evil for good. <hi type="super">22</hi> So and more also do God unto the enemies of David, if I leave of all that <hi type="italic">pertain</hi> to him by the morning light any that pisseth against the wall. <hi type="super">23</hi> And when Abigail saw David, she hasted, and lighted off the ass, and fell before David on her face, and bowed herself to the ground, <hi type="super">24</hi> And fell at his feet, and said, Upon me, my lord, <hi type="italic">upon</hi> me <hi type="italic">let this</hi> iniquity <hi type="italic">be:</hi> and let thine handmaid, I pray thee, speak in thine audience, and hear the words of thine handmaid. <hi type="super">25</hi> Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Nabal: for as his name <hi type="italic">is,</hi> so <hi type="italic">is</hi> he; Nabal <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name, and folly <hi type="italic">is</hi> with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send. <hi type="super">26</hi> Now therefore, my lord, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> thy soul liveth, seeing the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath withholden thee from coming to <hi type="italic">shed</hi> blood, and from avenging thyself with thine own hand, now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal. <hi type="super">27</hi> And now this blessing which thine handmaid hath brought unto my lord, let it even be given unto the young men that follow my lord. <hi type="super">28</hi> I pray thee, forgive the trespass of thine handmaid: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will certainly make my lord a sure house; because my lord fighteth the battles of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and evil hath not been found in thee <hi type="italic">all</hi> thy days. <hi type="super">29</hi> Yet a man is risen to pursue thee, and to seek thy soul: but the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God; and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out, <hi type="italic">as out</hi> of the middle of a sling. <hi type="super">30</hi> And it shall come to pass, when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall have done to my lord according to all the good that he hath spoken concerning thee, and shall have appointed thee ruler over Israel; <hi type="super">31</hi> That this shall be no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord, either that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself: but when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall have dealt well with my lord, then remember thine handmaid. <div eID="gen5804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5805" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of Abigail's prudent management for the preserving of her husband and family from the destruction that was just coming upon them; and we find that she did her part admirably well and fully answered her character. The passion of fools often makes those breaches in a little time which the wise, with all their wisdom, have much ado to make up again. It is hard to say whether Abigail was more miserable in such a husband or Nabal happy in such a wife. A <hi type="italic">virtuous woman is a crown to her husband,</hi> to protect as well as adorn, and will <hi type="italic">do him good and not evil.</hi> Wisdom in such a case as this was better than weapons of war. 1. It was her wisdom that what she did she did quickly, and without delay; she made haste, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">v. 18</reference>. It was no time to trifle or linger when all was in danger. Those that desire conditions of peace must send when the enemy is yet a great way off, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.32">Luke xiv. 32</reference>. 2. It was her wisdom that what she did she did herself, because, being a woman of great prudence and very happy address, she knew better how to manage it than any servant she had. The virtuous woman will herself <hi type="italic">look well to the ways of her household,</hi> and not devolve this duty wholly upon others. <div eID="gen5805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5806" type="x-p"/> Abigail must endeavour to atone for Nabal's faults. Now he had been in two ways rude to David's messengers, and in them to David: He had denied them the provisions they asked for, and he had given them very provoking language. Now, <div eID="gen5806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> I. By a most generous present, Abigail atones for his denial of their request. If Nabal had given them what came next to hand, they would have gone away thankful; but Abigail prepares the very best the house afforded and abundance of it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">v. 18</reference>), according to the usual entertainments of those times, not only <hi type="italic">bread</hi> and <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> but <hi type="italic">raisins</hi> and <hi type="italic">figs,</hi> which were their dried sweet-meats. Nabal grudged them <hi type="italic">water,</hi> but she took <hi type="italic">two bottles</hi> (<hi type="italic">casks</hi> or <hi type="italic">rundlets</hi>) <hi type="italic">of wine,</hi> loaded her asses with these provisions, and sent them before; for <hi type="italic">a gift pacifieth anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.14">Prov. xxi. 14</reference>. Jacob thus pacified Esau. When the <hi type="italic">instruments of the churl are evil, the liberal devises liberal things,</hi> and loses nothing by it; for by <hi type="italic">liberal things shall he stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.7-Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 7, 8</reference>. Abigail not only lawfully, but laudably, disposed of all these goods of her husband's without his knowledge (even when she had reason to think that if he had known what she did he would not have consented to it), because it was not to gratify her own pride or vanity, but for the necessary defence of him and his family. which otherwise would have been inevitably ruined. Husbands and wives, for their common good and benefit, have a joint-interest in their worldly possessions; but if either waste, or unduly spend in any way, it is a robbing of the other. <div eID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5808" type="x-p"/> II. By a most obliging demeanour, and charming speech, she atones for the abusive language which Nabal had given them. She met David upon the march, big with resentment, and meditating the destruction of Nabal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.20">v. 20</reference>); but with all possible expressions of complaisance and respect she humbly begs his favour, and solicits him to pass by the offence. Her demeanour was very submissive: <hi type="italic">She bowed herself to the ground before David</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.23">v. 23</reference>) <hi type="italic">and fell at his feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.24">v. 24</reference>. Yielding pacifies great offences. She put herself into the place and posture of a penitent and of a petitioner, and was not ashamed to do it, when it was for the good of her house, in the sight both of her own servants and of David's soldiers. She humbly begs of David that he will give her the hearing: <hi type="italic">Let thy handmaid speak in thy audience.</hi> But she needed not thus to bespeak his attention and patience; what she said was sufficient to command it, for certainly nothing could be more fine nor more moving. No topic of argument is left untouched; every thing is well placed and well expressed, most pertinently and pathetically urged, and improved to the best advantage, with such a force of natural rhetoric as cannot easily be paralleled. <div eID="gen5808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5809" type="x-p"/> 1. She speaks to him all along with the deference and respect due to so great and good a man, calls him <hi type="italic">My lord,</hi> over and over, to expiate her husband's crime in saying, "Who is David?" She does not upbraid him with the heat of his passion, though he deserved to be reproved for it; nor does she tell him how ill it became his character; but endeavours to soften him and bring him to a better temper, not doubting but that then his own conscience would upbraid him with it. <div eID="gen5809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5810" type="x-p"/> 2. She takes the blame of the ill-treatment of his messengers upon herself: "<hi type="italic">Upon me, my lord, upon me, let this iniquity be,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.24">v. 24</reference>. If thou wilt be angry, be angry with me, rather than with my poor husband, and look upon it <hi type="italic">as the trespass of thy handmaid,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.28">v. 28</reference>. Sordid spirits care not how much others suffer for their faults, while generous spirits can be content to suffer for the faults of others. Abigail here discovered the sincerity and strength of her conjugal affection and concern for her family: whatever Nabal was, he was her husband. <div eID="gen5810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5811" type="x-p"/> 3. She excuses her husband's fault by imputing it to his natural weakness and want of understanding (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let not my lord</hi> take notice of his rudeness and ill manners, for it is like him; it is not the first time that he has behaved so churlishly; he must be borne with, for it is for want of wit: <hi type="italic">Nabal is his name</hi>" (which signifies a <hi type="italic">fool</hi>), "<hi type="italic">and folly is with him.</hi> It was owing to his folly, not his malice. He is simple, but not spiteful. Forgive him, for he knows not what he does." What she said was too true, and she said it to excuse his fault and prevent his ruin, else she would not have done well to give such a bad character as this of her own husband, whom she ought to make the best of, and not to speak ill of. <div eID="gen5811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5812" type="x-p"/> 4. She pleads her own ignorance of the matter: "<hi type="italic">I saw not the young men,</hi> else they should have had a better answer, and should not have gone without their errand," intimating hereby that though her husband was foolish, and unfit to manage his affairs himself, yet he had so much wisdom as to be ruled by her and take her advice. <div eID="gen5812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5813" type="x-p"/> 5. She takes it for granted that she has gained her point already, perhaps perceiving, by David's countenance, that he began to change his mind (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Seeing the Lord hath withholden thee.</hi> She depends not upon her own reasonings, but God's grace, to mollify him, and doubts not but that grace would work powerfully upon him; and then, "<hi type="italic">Let all thy enemies be as Nabal,</hi> that is, if thou forbear to avenge thyself, no doubt God will avenge thee on him, as he will on all thy other enemies." Or it intimates that it was below him to take vengeance on so weak and impotent an enemy as Nabal was, who, as he would do him no kindness, so he could do him no hurt, for he needed to wish no more concerning his enemies than that they might be as unable to resist him as Nabal was. Perhaps she refers to his sparing Saul, when, but the other day, he had him at his mercy. "Didst thou forbear to avenge thyself on that lion that would devour thee, and wilt thou shed the blood of this dog that can but bark at thee?" The very mentioning of what he was about to do, to shed blood and to avenge himself, was enough to work upon such a tender gracious spirit as David had; and it should seem, by his reply (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.33">v. 33</reference>), that it affected him. <div eID="gen5813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5814" type="x-p"/> 6. She makes a tender of the present she had brought, but speaks of it as unworthy of David's acceptance, and therefore desires it may be given to the <hi type="italic">young men that followed him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.27">v. 27</reference>), and particularly to those ten that were his messengers to Nabal, and whom he had treated so rudely. <div eID="gen5814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5815" type="x-p"/> 7. She applauds David for the good services he had done against the common enemies of his country, the glory of which great achievements, she hoped, he would not stain by any personal revenge: "<hi type="italic">My lord fighteth the battles of the Lord</hi> against the Philistines, and therefore he will leave it to God to fight his battles against those that affront him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.28">v. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Evil has not been found in thee all thy days.</hi> Thou never yet didst wrong to any of thy countrymen (though persecuted as a traitor), and therefore thou wilt not begin now, nor do a thing which Saul will improve for the justifying of his malice against thee." <div eID="gen5815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5816" type="x-p"/> 8. She foretels the glorious issue of his present troubles. "It is true <hi type="italic">a man pursues thee</hi> and <hi type="italic">seeks thy life</hi>" (she names not Saul, out of respect to his present character as king), "but thou needest not look with so sharp and jealous an eye upon every one that affronts thee;" for all these storms that now ruffle thee will be blown over shortly. She speaks it with assurance, (1.) That God would keep him safe: <hi type="italic">The soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God,</hi> that is, God shall <hi type="italic">hold thy soul in life</hi> (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.9">Ps. lxvi. 9</reference>) as we hold those things which are bundled up or which are precious to us, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.15">Ps. cxvi. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy soul shall be treasured up in the treasure of lives</hi> (so the Chaldee), under lock and key as our treasure is. "Thou shalt abide under the special protection of the divine providence." The <hi type="italic">bundle of life is with the Lord our God,</hi> for in his hand our breath is, and our times. Those are safe, and may be easy, that have him for their protector. The Jews understand this not only of the <hi type="italic">life that now is,</hi> but of that <hi type="italic">which is to come,</hi> even the happiness of separate souls, and therefore use it commonly as an inscription on their gravestones. "Here we have laid the body, but trust that <hi type="italic">the soul is bound up in the bundle of life, with the Lord our God.</hi>" There it is safe, while the dust of the body is scattered. (2.) That God would make him victorious over his enemies. Their souls he shall <hi type="italic">sling out,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">v. 29</reference>. The stone is bound up in the sling, but it is in order to be thrown out again; so the souls of the godly shall be bundled as corn for the barn, but the souls of the wicked as tares for the fire. (3.) That God would settle him in wealth and power: "<hi type="italic">The Lord will certainly make my lord a sure house,</hi> and no enemy thou hast can hinder it; therefore <hi type="italic">forgive this trespass,</hi>" that is, "show mercy, as thou hopest to find mercy. God will make thee great, and it is the glory of great men to pass by offences." <div eID="gen5816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> 9. She desires him to consider how much more comfortable it would be to him in the reflection to have forgiven this affront than to have revenged it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.30-1Sam.25.31">v. 30, 31</reference>. She reserves this argument for the last, as a very powerful one with so good a man, that the less he indulged his passion the more he consulted his peace and the repose of his own conscience, which every wise man will be tender of. (1.) She cannot but think that if he should avenge himself it would afterwards be a grief and an offence of heart to him, Many have done that in a heat which they have a thousand times wished undone again. The sweetness of revenge is soon turned into bitterness. (2.) She is confident that if he pass by the offence it will afterwards by no grief to him; but, on the contrary, it would yield him unspeakable satisfaction that his wisdom and grace had got the better of his passion. Note, When we are tempted to sin we should consider how it will appear in the reflection. Let us never do any thing for which our own consciences will afterwards have occasion to upbraid us, and which we shall look back upon with regret: <hi type="italic">My heart shall not reproach me.</hi> <div eID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> 10. She recommends herself to his favour: <hi type="italic">When the Lord shall have dealt well with my lord, then remember thy handmaid,</hi> as one that kept thee from doing that which would have disgraced thy honour, disquieted thy conscience, and made a blot in thy history. We have reason to remember those with respect and gratitude who have been instrumental to keep us from sin.
entries.f990d249650939f23d23a4c1f515cc7b556c1427: <div eID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Blesses Abigail. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5819" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> And David said to Abigail, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: <hi type="super">33</hi> And blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> thy advice, and blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to <hi type="italic">shed</hi> blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand. <hi type="super">34</hi> For in very deed, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel liveth, which hath kept me back from hurting thee, except thou hadst hasted and come to meet me, surely there had not been left unto Nabal by the morning light any that pisseth against the wall. <hi type="super">35</hi> So David received of her hand <hi type="italic">that</hi> which she had brought him, and said unto her, Go up in peace to thine house; see, I have hearkened to thy voice, and have accepted thy person. <div eID="gen5819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5820" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">As an ear-ring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.12">Prov. xxv. 12</reference>. Abigail was a wise reprover of David's passion, and he gave an obedient ear to the reproof, according to his own principle (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Ps. cxli. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let the righteous smite me, it shall be a kindness.</hi> Never was such an admonition either better given or better taken. <div eID="gen5820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> I. David gives God thanks for sending him this happy check to a sinful way (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent thee this day to meet me.</hi> Note, 1. God is to be acknowledged in all the kindnesses that our friends do us either for soul or body. Whoever meet us with counsel, direction, comfort, caution, or seasonable reproof, we must see God sending them. 2. We ought to be very thankful for those happy providences which are means of preventing sin. <div eID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5822" type="x-p"/> II. He gives Abigail thanks for interposing so opportunely between him and the mischief he was about to do: <hi type="italic">Blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.33">v. 33</reference>. Most people think it enough if they take a reproof patiently, but we meet with few that will take it thankfully and will commend those that give it to them and accept it as a favour. Abigail did not rejoice more that she had been instrumental to save her husband and family from death than David did that Abigail had been instrumental to save him and his men from sin. <div eID="gen5822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> III. He seems very apprehensive of the great danger he was in, which magnified the mercy of his deliverance. 1. He speaks of the sin as very great. He was coming to shed blood, a sin of which when in his right mind he had a great horror, witness his prayer, <hi type="italic">Deliver me from blood-guiltiness.</hi> He was coming to <hi type="italic">avenge himself with his own hand,</hi> and that would be stepping into the throne of God, who has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine; I will repay.</hi> The more heinous any sin is the greater mercy it is to be kept from it. He seems to aggravate the evil of his design with this, that it would have been an injury to so wise and good a woman as Abigail: God has <hi type="italic">kept me back from hurting thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.34">v. 34</reference>. Or perhaps, at the first sight of Abigail, he was conscious of a thought to do her a mischief for offering to oppose him, and therefore reckons it a great mercy that God gave him patience to hear her speak. 2. He speaks of the danger of his falling into it as very imminent: "<hi type="italic">Except thou hadst hasted,</hi> the bloody execution had been done." The nearer we were to the commission of sin the greater was the mercy of a seasonable restraint—<hi type="italic">Almost gone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Ps. lxxiii. 2</reference>) and yet upheld. <div eID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> IV. He dismissed her with an answer of peace, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.35">v. 35</reference>. He does, in effect, own himself overcome by her eloquence: "<hi type="italic">I have hearkened to thy voice,</hi> and will not prosecute the intended revenge, for I <hi type="italic">have accepted thy person,</hi> am well pleased with thee and what thou hast said." Note, 1. Wise and good men will hear reason, and let that rule them, though it come from those that are every way their inferiors, and though their passions are up and their spirits provoked. 2. Oaths cannot, bind us to that which is sinful. David had solemnly vowed the death of Nabal. He did evil to make such a vow, but he would have done worse if he had performed it. 3. A wise and faithful reproof is often better taken, and speeds better, than we expected, such is the hold God has of men's consciences. See <reference osisRef="Prov.28.23">Prov. xxviii. 23</reference>.
entries.30276e3e528780b4e7503a2bbf1530e411860ef9: <div eID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Marries Abigail. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5825" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> And Abigail came to Nabal; and, behold, he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king; and Nabal's heart <hi type="italic">was</hi> merry within him, for he <hi type="italic">was</hi> very drunken: wherefore she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light. <hi type="super">37</hi> But it came to pass in the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, and his wife had told him these things, that his heart died within him, and he became <hi type="italic">as</hi> a stone. <hi type="super">38</hi> And it came to pass about ten days <hi type="italic">after,</hi> that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> smote Nabal, that he died. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and hath kept his servant from evil: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. And David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife. <hi type="super">40</hi> And when the servants of David were come to Abigail to Carmel, they spake unto her, saying, David sent us unto thee, to take thee to him to wife. <hi type="super">41</hi> And she arose, and bowed herself on <hi type="italic">her</hi> face to the earth, and said, Behold, <hi type="italic">let</hi> thine handmaid <hi type="italic">be</hi> a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord. <hi type="super">42</hi> And Abigail hasted, and arose, and rode upon an ass, with five damsels of hers that went after her; and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife. <hi type="super">43</hi> David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel; and they were also both of them his wives. <hi type="super">44</hi> But Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> of Gallim. <div eID="gen5825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5826" type="x-p"/> We are now to attend Nabal's funeral and Abigail's wedding. <div eID="gen5826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5827" type="x-p"/> I. Nabal's funeral. The apostle speaks of some that were <hi type="italic">twice dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>. We have hare Nabal <hi type="italic">thrice</hi> dead, though but just now wonderfully rescued from the sword of David and delivered from so great a death; for the preservations of wicked men are but reservations for some further sorer strokes of divine wrath. Here is, <div eID="gen5827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5828" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Nabal dead drunk,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36">v. 36</reference>. Abigail came home, and, it should seem, he had so many people and so much plenty about him that he neither missed her nor the provisions she took to David; but she found him in the midst of his jollity, little thinking how near he was to ruin by one whom he had foolishly made his enemy. Sinners are often most secure when they are most in danger and destruction is at the door. Observe, (1.) How extravagant he was in the entertainment of his company: <hi type="italic">He held a feast like the feast of a king,</hi> so magnificent and abundant, though his guests were but his sheep-shearers. This abundance might have been allowed if he had considered what God gave him his estate for, not to look great with, but to do good with. It is very common for those that are most niggardly in any act of piety or charity to be most profuse in gratifying a vain humour or a base lust. A mite is grudged to God and his poor; but, to make a <hi type="italic">fair show in the flesh, gold is lavished out of the bag.</hi> If Nabal had not answered to his name, he would never have been thus secure and jovial, till he had enquired whether he was safe from David's resentments; but (as bishop Hall observes) thus foolish are carnal men, that give themselves over to their pleasures before they have taken any care to make their peace with God. (2.) How sottish he was in the indulgence of his own brutish appetite: <hi type="italic">He was very drunk,</hi> a sign he was <hi type="italic">Nabal, a fool,</hi> that could not use his plenty without abusing it, could not be pleasant with his friends without making a beast of himself. There is not a surer sign that a man has but little wisdom, nor a surer way to ruin the little he has, than drinking to excess. Nabal, that never thought he could bestow too little in charity, never thought he could bestow too much in luxury. Abigail, finding him in this condition (and probably those about him little better, when the master of the feast set them so bad an example), had enough to do to set the disordered house to-rights a little, but told Nabal nothing of what she had done with reference to David, nothing of his folly in provoking David, of his danger or of his deliverance, for, being drunk, he was as incapable to hear reason as he was to speak it. To give good advice to those that are in drink is to <hi type="italic">cast pearls before swine;</hi> it is better to stay till they are sober. <div eID="gen5828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5829" type="x-p"/> 2. Nabal again dead with melancholy, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.37">v. 37</reference>. Next morning, when he had come to himself a little, his wife told him how near to destruction he had brought himself and his family by his own rudeness, and with what difficulty she had interposed to prevent it; and, upon this, <hi type="italic">his heart died within him and he became as a stone.</hi> Some suggest that the expense of the satisfaction made to David, by the present Abigail brought him, broke his heart: it seems rather that the apprehension he now had of the danger he had narrowly escaped put him into a consternation, and seized his spirits so that he could not recover it. He grew sullen, and said little, ashamed of his own folly, put out of countenance by his wife's wisdom. How is he changed! His heart over-night merry with wine, next morning heavy as a stone; so deceitful are carnal pleasures, so transient the laughter of the fool. <hi type="italic">The end of that mirth is heaviness.</hi> Drunkards are sometimes sad when they reflect upon their own folly. Joy in God makes the heart always light. Abigail could never, by her wise reasonings, bring Nabal to repentance; but now, by her faithful reproof, she brings him to despair. <div eID="gen5829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5830" type="x-p"/> 3. Nabal, at last, dead indeed: <hi type="italic">About ten days after,</hi> when he had been kept so long under this pressure and pain, <hi type="italic">the Lord smote him that he died</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.38">v. 38</reference>), and, it should seem, he never held up his head; it is just with God (says bishop Hall) that those who live without grace should die without comfort, nor can we expect better while we go on in our sins. Here is no lamentation made for Nabal. He departed without being lamented. Every one wished that the country might never sustain a greater loss. <hi type="italic">David,</hi> when he heard the news of his death, <hi type="italic">gave God thanks</hi> for it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.39">v. 39</reference>. He blessed God, (1.) That he had kept him from killing him: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the lord, who hath kept his servant from evil.</hi> He rejoices that Nabal died a natural death and not by his hand. We should take all occasions to mention and magnify God's goodness to us in keeping us from sin. (2.) That he had taken the work into his own hands, and had vindicated David's honour, and not suffered him to go unpunished who had been abusive to him; hereby his interest would be confirmed, and all would stand in awe of him, as one for whom God fought. (3.) That he had thereby encouraged him and all others to commit their cause to God, when they are in any way injured, with an assurance that, in his own time, he will redress their wrongs if they sit still and leave the matter to him. <div eID="gen5830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5831" type="x-p"/> II. Abigail's wedding. David was so charmed with the beauty of her person, and the uncommon prudence of her conduct and address, that, as soon as was convenient, after he heard she was a widow, he informed her of his attachment to her (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.39">v. 39</reference>), not doubting but that she who approved herself so good a wife to so bad a husband as Nabal would much more make a good wife to him, and having taken notice of her respect to him and her confidence of his coming to the throne. 1. He courted by proxy, his affairs, perhaps, not permitting him to come himself. 2. She received the address with great modesty and humility (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.41">v. 41</reference>), reckoning herself unworthy of the honour, yet having such a respect for him that she would gladly be one of the poorest servants of his family, to wash the feet of the other servants. None so fit to be preferred as those that can thus humble themselves. 3. She agreed to the proposal, went with his messenger, took a retinue with her agreeable to her quality, and <hi type="italic">she became his wife,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.42">v. 42</reference>. She did not upbraid him with his present distresses, and ask him how he could maintain her, but valued him, (1.) Because she knew he was a very good man. (2.) Because she believed he would, in due time, be a very great man. She married him in faith, not questioning but that, though now he had not a house of his own that he durst bring her to, yet God's promise go him would at length be fulfilled. Thus those who join themselves to Christ must be willing now to suffer with him, believing that hereafter they shall reign with him. <div eID="gen5831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5832" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> On this occasion we have some account of David's wives. 1. One that he had lost before he married Abigail, Michal, Saul's daughter, his first, and the wife of his youth, to whom he would have been constant if she would have been so to him, but Saul had given her to another (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.44">v. 44</reference>), in token of his displeasure against him and disclaiming the relation of a father-in-law to him. 2. Another that he married besides Abigail (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.43">v. 43</reference>), and, as should seem, before her, for she is named first, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.3">ch. xxvii. 3</reference>. David was carried away by the corrupt custom of those times; but from the beginning it was not so, nor is it so now that Messias has come, and the times of reformation, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.4-Matt.19.5">Matt. xix. 4, 5</reference>. Perhaps Saul's defrauding David of his only rightful wife was the occasion of his running into this irregularity; for, when the knot of conjugal affection is once loosed, it is scarcely ever tied fast again. When David could not keep his first wife he thought that would excuse him if he did not keep to his second. But we deceive ourselves if we think to make others' faults a cloak for our own.  <chapter eID="1Sam.25"/> <div eID="gen5832" type="x-p"/>

entries.ea0aa96f3115f26db58f44aaec5e2d4996e277f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2760"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <div sID="gen3772" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1-1Sam.25.9">1Sa 25:1-9</reference>. Samuel Dies.<div eID="gen3772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2760"/><hi type="bold">1. Samuel died--</hi>After a long life of piety and public usefulness, he left behind him a reputation which ranks him among the greatest of Scripture worthies.<div eID="gen3773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buried him in his house at Ramah--</hi>that is, his own mausoleum. The Hebrews took as great care to provide sepulchers anciently as people do in the East still, where every respectable family has its own house of the dead. Often this is in a little detached garden, containing a small stone building (where there is no rock), resembling a house, which is called the sepulcher of the family--it has neither door nor window.<div eID="gen3774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David arose, and went down to the wilderness of Paran--</hi>This removal had probably no connection with the prophet's death; but was probably occasioned by the necessity of seeking provision for his numerous followers.<div eID="gen3775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wilderness of Paran--</hi>stretching from Sinai to the borders of Palestine in the southern territories of Judea. Like other wildernesses, it presented large tracts of natural pasture, to which the people sent their cattle at the grazing season, but where they were liable to constant and heavy depredations by prowling Arabs. David and his men earned their subsistence by making reprisals on the cattle of these freebooting Ishmaelites; and, frequently for their useful services, they obtained voluntary tokens of acknowledgment from the peaceful inhabitants. <div eID="gen3776" type="x-p"/>
entries.2123c8173a124d61eb1edfdc975cf92135dababf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2761"/><div sID="gen3777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2761"/><hi type="bold">2. in Carmel--</hi>now Kurmul. The district takes its name from this town, now a mass of ruins; and about a mile from it is Tell Main, the hillock on which stood ancient Maon.<div eID="gen3777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man was very great--</hi>His property consisted in cattle, and he was considered wealthy, according to the ideas of that age. <div eID="gen3778" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb94a24e84183e61a164f2913e81b63d132fbc3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2762"/><div sID="gen3779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2762"/><hi type="bold">3. he was of the house of Caleb--</hi>of course, of the same tribe with David himself; but many versions consider Caleb ("dog") not as a proper, but a common noun, and render it, "he was snappish as a dog." <div eID="gen3779" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6e252491cd45d03435a895d29d78c4fb0d647ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2763"/><div sID="gen3780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2763"/><hi type="bold">4-9. Nabal did shear his sheep, and David sent out ten young men, &c.--</hi>David and his men lurked in these deserts, associating with the herdsmen and shepherds of Nabal and others and doing them good offices, probably in return for information and supplies obtained through them. Hence when Nabal held his annual sheep-shearing in Carmel, David felt himself entitled to share in the festival and sent a message, recounting his own services and asking for a present. "In all these particulars we were deeply struck with the truth and strength of the biblical description of manners and customs almost identically the same as they exist at the present day. On such a festive occasion, near a town or village, even in our own time, an Arab sheik of the neighboring desert would hardly fail to put in a word either in person or by message; and his message, both in form and substance, would be only a transcript of that of David" [Robinson].<div eID="gen3780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3781" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.10-1Sam.25.13">1Sa 25:10-13</reference>. The Churlish Answer Provokes Him. <div eID="gen3781" type="x-p"/>
entries.5eb580129f2ea54b8bda1b161d419f60003efe74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2764"/><div sID="gen3782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2764"/><hi type="bold">10-12. Nabal answered David's servants, ... Who is David? &c.--</hi>Nabal's answer seems to indicate that the country was at the time in a loose and disorderly state. David's own good conduct, however, as well as the important services rendered by him and his men, were readily attested by Nabal's servants. The preparations of David to chastise his insolent language and ungrateful requital are exactly what would be done in the present day by Arab chiefs, who protect the cattle of the large and wealthy sheep masters from the attacks of the marauding border tribes or wild beasts. Their protection creates a claim for some kind of tribute, in the shape of supplies of food and necessaries, which is usually given with great good will and gratitude; but when withheld, is enforced as a right. Nabal's refusal, therefore, was a violation of the established usages of the place. <div eID="gen3782" type="x-p"/>
entries.88a29c671146152ab238a1d034aeb4cd455187d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2765"/><div sID="gen3783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2765"/><hi type="bold">13. two hundred abode by the stuff--</hi>This addition to his followers was made after his return into Judah (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.2">1Sa 22:2</reference>).<div eID="gen3783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3784" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.14-1Sam.25.35">1Sa 25:14-35</reference>. Abigail Pacifies Him. <div eID="gen3784" type="x-p"/>
entries.163f3c73ebc74a21a64c104b1991fc655f2168b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2766"/><div sID="gen3785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2766"/><hi type="bold">14-18. Then Abigail made haste--</hi>The prudence and address of Nabal's wife were the means of saving him and family from utter destruction. She acknowledged the demand of her formidable neighbors; but justly considering, that to atone for the insolence of her husband, a greater degree of liberality had become necessary, she collected a large amount of food, accompanying it with the most valued products of the country.<div eID="gen3785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bottles--</hi>goatskins, capable of holding a great quantity.<div eID="gen3786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">parched corn--</hi>It was customary to eat parched corn when it was fully grown, but not ripe. <div eID="gen3787" type="x-p"/>
entries.56a82c64a5a9ec69cf11a244bbf4ed0e4f8fdd6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2767"/><div sID="gen3788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2767"/><hi type="bold">19. she said unto her servants, Go on before me; behold, I come after you--</hi>People in the East always try to produce an effect by their presents, loading on several beasts what might be easily carried by one, and bringing them forward, article by article, in succession. Abigail not only sent her servants in this way, but resolved to go in person, following her present, as is commonly done, to watch the impression which her munificence would produce. <div eID="gen3788" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a67843d34e6e12f212205ce5a18deb774c937d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2768"/><div sID="gen3789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2768"/><hi type="bold">23. she hasted, and lighted off the ass, and fell before David on her face--</hi>Dismounting in presence of a superior is the highest token of respect that can be given; and it is still an essential act of homage to the great. Accompanying this act of courtesy with the lowest form of prostration, she not only by her attitude, but her language, made the fullest amends for the disrespect shown by her husband, as well as paid the fullest tribute of respect to the character and claims of David. <div eID="gen3789" type="x-p"/>
entries.fabd9c225bae416184c5da6a7612d8640ad3a39d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2769"/><div sID="gen3790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2769"/><hi type="bold">25. Nabal--</hi>signifying fool, gave pertinence to his wife's remark. <div eID="gen3790" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee7586f89ba5edabef808ac8676c2f6a6f06a41a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2770"/><div sID="gen3791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2770"/><hi type="bold">26. let thine enemies ... be as Nabal--</hi>be as foolish and contemptible as he. <div eID="gen3791" type="x-p"/>
entries.f11cc823996b03e3230cf54482dce00b75ca566c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2771"/><div sID="gen3792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2771"/><hi type="bold">29. the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God--</hi>An Orientalism, expressing the perfect security of David's life from all the assaults of his enemies, under the protecting shield of Providence, who had destined him for high things. <div eID="gen3792" type="x-p"/>
entries.e15ed74439fc89c61fb06cbf9d2987c8596b75e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2772"/><div sID="gen3793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2772"/><hi type="bold">32-35. David said to Abigail, Blessed be the Lord--</hi>Transported by passion and blinded by revenge, he was on the eve of perpetrating a great injury. Doubtless, the timely appearance and prudent address of Abigail were greatly instrumental in changing his purpose. At all events, it was the means of opening his eyes to the moral character of the course on which he had been impetuously rushing; and in accepting her present, he speaks with lively satisfaction as well as gratitude to Abigail, for having relieved him from bloodshed.<div eID="gen3793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3794" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36-1Sam.25.44">1Sa 25:36-44</reference>. Nabal's Death. <div eID="gen3794" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2053a6ff475e658f091b3d7bcaf62b27ad29b13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2773"/><div sID="gen3795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2773"/><hi type="bold">36. he held a feast in his house, like the feast of a king--</hi>The sheep-shearing season was always a very joyous occasion. Masters usually entertained their shepherds; and even Nabal, though of a most niggardly disposition, prepared festivities on a scale of sumptuous liberality. The modern Arabs celebrate the season with similar hilarity. <div eID="gen3795" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5c4b13874ffd5a3ec87b90c6644e6d3409cd40b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2774"/><div sID="gen3796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2774"/><hi type="bold">37-38. in the morning ... his wife had told him these things, that his heart died within him--</hi>He probably fainted from horror at the perilous situation in which he had unconsciously placed himself; and such a shock had been given him by the fright to his whole system, that he rapidly pined and died. <div eID="gen3796" type="x-p"/>
entries.a86f3fb2000c5787f263f261a62d4d8562919401: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2775"/><div sID="gen3797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2775"/><hi type="bold">39-42. the Lord hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head--</hi>If this was an expression of pleasure, and David's vindictive feelings were gratified by the intelligence of Nabal's death, it was an instance of human infirmity which we may lament; but perhaps he referred to the unmerited reproach (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.10">1Sa 25:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.11">11</reference>), and the contempt of God implied in it.<div eID="gen3797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to wife--</hi>This unceremonious proceeding was quite in the style of Eastern monarchs, who no sooner take a fancy for a lady than they despatch a messenger to intimate their royal wishes that she should henceforth reside in the palace; and her duty is implicitly to obey. David's conduct shows that the manners of the Eastern nations were already imitated by the great men in Israel; and that the morality of the times which God permitted, gave its sanction to the practice of polygamy. His marriage with Abigail brought him a rich estate. <div eID="gen3798" type="x-p"/>
entries.60bc46535f4dcd2d438b33b51353af946e0845d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2776"/><div sID="gen3799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2776"/><hi type="bold">44. Michal--</hi>By the unchallengeable will of her father, she who was David's wife was given to another. But she returned and sustained the character of his wife when he ascended the throne. <chapter eID="1Sam.25"/>

entries.a046e2684f10ce2bddd676012ab5e70d962d9d51: <div eID="gen10413" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10414" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10415" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10415" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10414" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10416" type="x-p"/> The death of Samuel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">1Sam 25:1</reference>. The history of Nabal, and his churlishness towards David and his men, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2-1Sam.25.12">1Sam 25:2-12</reference>. David, determining to punish him, is appeased by Abigail, Nabal's wife, vv. 13-35. Abigail returns, and tells Nabal of the danger that he has escaped: who on hearing it is thunderstruck, and dies in ten days, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36-1Sam.25.38">1Sam 25:36-38</reference> David, hearing of this, sends and takes Abigail to wife, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.39-1Sam.25.42">1Sam 25:39-42</reference>. He marries also Ahinoam of Jezreel, Saul having given Michal, David's wife, to Phalti, the son of Laish, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.43">1Sam 25:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.44">1Sam 25:44</reference>. <div eID="gen10416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10418" type="x-p"/> And Samuel died - Samuel lived, as is supposed, about ninety-eight years; was in the government of Israel before Saul from sixteen to twenty years; and ceased to live, according to the Jews, about four months before the death of Saul; but according to Calmet and others, two years. But all this is very uncertain; how long he died before Saul, cannot be ascertained. For some account of his character, see the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.44">1Sam 25:44</reference> (note). <div eID="gen10418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10419" type="x-p"/> Buried him in his house - Probably this means, not his dwelling-house, but the house or tomb he had made for his sepulture; and thus the Syriac and Arabic seem to have understood it. <div eID="gen10419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10420" type="x-p"/> David - went down to the wilderness of Paran - This was either on the confines of Judea, or in Arabia Petraea, between the mountains of Judah and Mount Sinai; it is evident from the history that it was not far from Carmel, on the south confines of Judah.
