entries.00333b8f87c397feeef0238848696119fdb30d19: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10421" type="x-p"/> The name of the man was Nabal - The word נבל nabal signifies to be foolish, base, or villanous; and hence the Latin word nebulo, knave, is supposed to be derived. <div eID="gen10421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10422" type="x-p"/> The name of his wife Abigail - The joy or exultation of my father. A woman of sense and beauty, married to the boor mentioned above, probably because he was rich. Many women have been thus sacrificed. <div eID="gen10422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10423" type="x-p"/> Of the house of Caleb - והוא כלבי vehu Chalibbi, "he was a Calebite." But as the word caleb signifies a dog, the Septuagint have understood it as implying a man of a canine disposition, and translate it thus, και ὁ ανθρωπος κυνικος, he was a doggish man. It is understood in the same way by the Syriac and Arabic.
entries.b5d19e03f9e9b67ea5b1e37092b8b665e5d469e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10424" type="x-p"/> Peace be both to thee - This is the ancient form of sending greetings to a friend: Peace to Thee, peace to thy Household, and peace to all that Thou Hast. That is, May both thyself, thy family, and all that pertain unto thee, be in continual prosperity! <div eID="gen10424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10425" type="x-p"/> Perhaps David, by this salutation, wished Nabal to understand that he had acted so towards him and his property that nothing had been destroyed, and that all had been protected; see <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.15-1Sam.25.17">1Sam 25:15-17</reference>.
entries.2b4a363e9041c273d2ce1b3ca1c20b7b104213d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10426" type="x-p"/> Thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not - It is most evident that David had a claim upon Nabal, for very essential services performed to his herdmen at Carmel. He not only did them no hurt, and took none of their flocks for the supply of his necessities, but he protected them from the rapacity of others; they were a Wall unto us, said Nabal's servants, both by night and day. In those times, and to the present day, wandering hordes of Arabs, under their several chiefs, think they have a right to exact contributions of provisions, etc., wherever they come; David had done nothing of this kind, but protected them against those who would.
entries.8f85da063128a8a27766a91e18672bbcbdf0f158: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10427" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever cometh to thine hand - As thou art making a great feast for thy servants, and I and my men, as having essentially served thee, would naturally come in for a share were we present; send a portion by my ten young men, for me and my men, that we also may rejoice with you. Certainly this was a very reasonable and a very modest request. This mode of address is not unfrequent among the Hindoos: "O father, fill the belly of thy son; he is in distress."
entries.6364209dcd03f76f58ac6c1fdb6a0e3762bbda53: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10428" type="x-p"/> Who is David? - Nabal's answer shows the surliness of his disposition. It was unjust to refuse so reasonable a request; and the manner of the refusal was highly insulting. It is true what his own servants said of him, He is such a son of Belial that one cannot speak to him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.17">1Sam 25:17</reference>.
entries.b82da03b33f550e24d697ec94d5653211e00fe58: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10429" type="x-p"/> Took two hundred loaves - The Eastern bread is ordinarily both thin and small; and answers to our cakes. <div eID="gen10429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10430" type="x-p"/> Two bottles of wine - That is, two goat-skins full. The hide is pulled off the animal without ripping up; the places where the legs, etc., were are sewed up, and then the skin appears one large bag. This is properly the Scripture and Eastern bottle. There is one such before me. <div eID="gen10430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10431" type="x-p"/> Five sheep - Not one sheep to one hundred men. <div eID="gen10431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10432" type="x-p"/> Clusters of raisins - Raisins dried in the sun. <div eID="gen10432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10433" type="x-p"/> Cakes of figs - Figs cured, and then pressed together. We receive the former in jars, and the latter in small barrels; and both articles answer the description here given. <div eID="gen10433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10434" type="x-p"/> Now all this provision was a matter of little worth, and, had it been granted in the first instance, it would have perfectly satisfied David, and secured the good offices of him and his men. Abigail showed both her wisdom and prudence in making this provision. Out of three thousand sheep Nabal could not have missed five; and as this claim was made only in the time of sheep-shearing, it could not have been made more than once in the year: and it certainly was a small price for such important services.
entries.5491c968f7dd70a61f693a4acf8a3bddfb57956e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen10434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10435" type="x-p"/> She came down - and David - came down - David was coming down Mount Paran; Abigail was coming down from Carmel. - Calmet.
entries.5b6565b7a5aa4bca337687b6594da24b1de76985: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen10435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10436" type="x-p"/> So and more also do God - Nothing can justify this part of David's conduct. Whatever his provocation might have been, he had suffered, properly speaking, no wrongs; and his resolution to cut off a whole innocent family, because Nabal had acted ungenerously towards him, was abominable and cruel, not to say diabolic. He who attempts to vindicate this conduct of David is, at least constructively, a foe to God and truth. David himself condemns this most rash and unwarrantable conduct, and thanks God for having prevented him from doing this evil, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.32">1Sam 25:32</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen10436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10437" type="x-p"/> Any that pisseth against the wall - This expression certainly means either men or dogs, and should be thus translated, if I leave, any male; and this will answer both to men and dogs, and the offensive mode of expression be avoided. I will not enter farther into the subject: Bochart and Calmet have done enough, and more than enough; and in the plainest language too.
entries.b0df82d1b30fb2d05d036d32a004d3825b8eba41: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen10437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10438" type="x-p"/> And evil hath not been found in thee - Thou hast not committed any act of this kind hitherto.
entries.f8d7dcb28f4b3216fcd147a693f42999a43fcdae: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen10438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10439" type="x-p"/> Shall be bound in the bundle of life - Thy life shall be precious in the sight of the Lord: it shall be found in the bundle of life; it shall be supported by Him who is the Spring and Fountain of life, and ever be found united to those who are most favored by the Almighty. <div eID="gen10439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10440" type="x-p"/> Them shall he sling out - Far from being bound and kept together in union with the Fountain of life, he will cast them off from himself as a stone is cast out from a sling. This betokens both force and violence.
entries.5942afe695adc7a88641ce8d7e5e0de1731bbf83: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen10440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10441" type="x-p"/> His heart died within him, and he became as a stone - He was thunderstruck, and was so terrified at the apprehension of what he had escaped, that the fear overcame his mind, he became insensible to all things around him, probably refused all kinds of nourishment, and died in ten days.
entries.49bb2db807a65d468fca6758c51f63c091624f63: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen10441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10442" type="x-p"/> To take her to him to wife - It is likely that he had heard before this that Saul, to cut off all his pretensions to the throne, had married Michal to Phalti; and this justified David in taking Abigail or any other woman; and, according to the then custom, it was not unlawful for David to take several wives. By his marriage with Abigail, it is probable he became possessed of all Nabal's property in Carmel and Maon.
entries.b670c809b4cc112a81ee346bfcbf71aeb5889e17: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen10442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10443" type="x-p"/> David also took Ahinoam - Many think that this was his wife before he took Abigail; she is always mentioned first in the list of his wives, and she was the mother of his eldest son Ammon. <div eID="gen10443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10444" type="x-p"/> Of Jezreel - There were two places of this name; one in the tribe of Issachar, the other in the tribe of Judah.
entries.8adb02250b8bcb0a33a6ada0d4ef60683f67c506: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen10444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10445" type="x-p"/> Phalti - Called also Phaltiel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.16">2Sam 3:16</reference>. <div eID="gen10445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10446" type="x-p"/> Of Gallim - Probably a city or town in the tribe of Benjamin; see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.30">Isa 10:30</reference>. It is likely therefore that Saul chose this man because he was of his own tribe. <div eID="gen10446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10447" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have the account of the death of Samuel, who from his infancy had been devoted to God and the service of his people. He was born at a time in which religion was at a very low ebb in Israel, as there were but very few prophets, and no open vision - scarcely any revelation from God. Those who might be called prophets had no regular ministry of God's word; they were extraordinary messengers sent for a particular purpose, and not continued in the work any longer than the time necessary to deliver their extraordinary message. <div eID="gen10447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10448" type="x-p"/> Samuel is supposed to have been the first who established academies or schools for prophets, at least we do not hear of them before his time; and it is granted that they continued till the Babylonish captivity. This was a wise institution, and no doubt contributed much to the maintenance of pure religion, and the prevention of idolatry among that people. <div eID="gen10448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10449" type="x-p"/> Samuel reformed many abuses in the Jewish state, and raised it to a pitch of political consequence to which it had been long a stranger. He was very zealous for the honor of God, and supported the rights of pure religion, of the king, and of the people, against all encroachments. He was chief magistrate in Israel before the appointment of a king, and afterwards he acted as prime minister to Saul, though without being chosen or formally appointed to that station. Indeed, he seems on the whole to have been the civil and ecclesiastical governor, Saul being little more than general of the Israelitish forces. <div eID="gen10449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10450" type="x-p"/> In his office of minister in the state, he gave the brightest example of zeal, diligence, inflexible integrity, and uncorruptedness. He reproved both the people and the king for their transgressions, with a boldness which nothing but his sense of the Divine authority could inspire, and yet he tempered it with a sweetness which showed the interest he felt in their welfare, and the deep and distressing concern he felt for their back-slidings and infidelities. <div eID="gen10450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10451" type="x-p"/> He was incorrupt; he received no man's bribe; he had no pension from the state; he enriched none of his relatives from the public purse; left no private debts to be discharged by his country. He was among the Hebrews what Aristides is said to have been among the Greeks, so poor at his death, though a minister of state, that he did not leave property enough to bury him. Justice was by him duly and impartially administered, and oppression and wrong had no existence. <div eID="gen10451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10452" type="x-p"/> If there ever was a heaven-born minister, it was Samuel; in whose public and private conduct there was no blemish, and whose parallel cannot be found in the ancient or modern history of any country in the universe. <div eID="gen10452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10453" type="x-p"/> Let ministers of state who have sought for nothing but their own glory, and have increased the public burdens by their improvident expenditure; who have endeavored, by their wordy representations, to dazzle and elude the people, and impose false grandeur in the place of true greatness and solid prosperity; who have oppressed the many, and enriched the worthless few; fall down at the feet of This heaven-born man, and learn, from this immaculate judge of Israel, what a faithful servant to his king, and an incorruptible minister of state, means, and in retiring from their high station, or in going to appear before the judgment-seat of God, see whether, in the presence of their king, and in the face of the thousands of their people, they can boldly say, "Behold, here am I! Witness against me before the Lord and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose ass have I seized? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed, by the imposition of heavy taxes for the support of needless expenses, and the payment of venal men? Or of whose hand have I taken any bribe to blind my eyes? Scrutinize my conduct, examine the state of my family, compare their present circumstances with what they were previously to my administration, and see if you can find aught in my hands." See <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.1">1Sam 12:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen10453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10454" type="x-p"/> O, how seldom in the annals of the world, from the assembled heads of the great body politic, can the departing prime minister hear, "Thou hast not defrauded us, thou hast not oppressed us; neither hast thou taken aught of any man's hand!" This voice call be heard from Gilgal; but of what other minister can this be spoken but of Samuel the seer, who was the gift of God's mercy to the people of Israel; whose memory was too precious to be intrusted to public monuments, but stands, and alas; almost unique in the Book of God? Of Daniel, and his administration, I shall have occasion to speak elsewhere. <div eID="gen10454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10455" type="x-p"/> A prime minister, deeply devoted to God and faithful to his king and to his country, is so rare a character in the world, that when he does occur, he should be held up to public admiration. But I have no parallel for Samuel. See the notes on 1 Samuel 12:1-25 (note) and on <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.6">1Sam 24:6</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="1Sam.25"/> <div eID="gen10455" type="x-p"/>

entries.76f99fb86bae60936bd1014e627a2ba765fde5de: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">1Sa  25:1</reference> <div eID="gen4095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4096" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">death of Samuel</hi> is inserted here, because it occurred at that time. The fact that all Israel assembled together to his burial, and lamented him, i.e., mourned for him, was a sign that his labours as a prophet were recognised by the whole nation as a blessing for Israel. Since the days of Moses and Joshua, no man had arisen to whom the covenant nation owed so much as to Samuel, who has been justly called the reformer and restorer of the theocracy. They buried him “<hi type="italic">in his house at Ramah</hi>.” The expression “his house” does not mean his burial-place or family tomb, nor his native place, but the house in which he lived, with the court belonging to it, where Samuel was placed in a tomb erected especially for him. After the death of Samuel, David went down into the desert of <hi type="italic">Paran</hi>, i.e., into the northern portion of the desert of Arabia, which stretches up to the mountains of Judah (see at Num 10:12); most likely for no other reason than because he could no longer find sufficient means of subsistence for himself and his six hundred men in the desert of Judah. <div eID="gen4096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4097" type="x-p"/> The following history of <hi type="italic">Nabal's</hi> folly, and of the wise and generous behaviour of his pious and intelligent wife Abigail towards David, shows how Jehovah watched over His servant David, and not only preserved him from an act of passionate excitement, which might have endangered his calling to be king of Israel, but turned the trouble into which he had been brought into a source of prosperity and salvation.
entries.2e9ed83d2e3520d9006fb26f6b571857ecfdd989: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2-1Sam.25.3">1Sa 25:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen4097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4098" type="x-p"/> At <hi type="italic">Maon</hi>, i.e., Main or the mountains of Judah (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>), there lived a rich man (גּדול, <hi type="italic">great</hi> through property and riches), who had his establishment at <hi type="italic">Carmel</hi>. מעשׂה, work, occupation, then establishment, possessions (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.23.15">Exo 23:15</reference>). <hi type="italic">Carmel</hi> is not the promontory of that name (Thenius), but the present <hi type="italic">Kurmul</hi> on the mountains of Judah, scarcely half an hour’s journey to the north-west of Maon (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>). This man possessed three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, and was at the sheep-shearing at Carmel. His name was <hi type="italic">Nabal</hi> (i.e., fool): this was hardly his proper name, but was a surname by which he was popularly designated on account of his folly. His wife <hi type="italic">Abigail</hi> was “<hi type="italic">of good understanding</hi>,” i.e., intelligent, “<hi type="italic">and of beautiful figure</hi>;” but the husband was “<hi type="italic">harsh and evil in his doings</hi>.” He sprang from the family of <hi type="italic">Caleb</hi>. This is the rendering adopted by the Chaldee and Vulgate, according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> כּלבּי. The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> is to be read כּלבּו, “according to his heart;” though the lxx (ἄνθρωπος κυνικός) and Josephus, as well as the Arabic and Syriac, derive it from כּלב, and understand it as referring to the dog-like, or shameless, character of the man.
entries.4a022cfea416ea92b34b8e9a3eb6c0da62992da7: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.4-1Sam.25.8">1Sa 25:4-8</reference> <div eID="gen4098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4099" type="x-p"/> When David heard in the desert (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">1Sa 25:1</reference>) that Nabal was shearing his sheep, which was generally accompanied with a festal meal (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.38.12">Gen 38:12</reference>), he sent ten young men up to Carmel to him, and bade them wish him peace and prosperity in his name, and having reminded him of the friendly services rendered to his shepherds, solicit a present for himself and his people. לשׁלום לו שׁאל, ask him after his welfare, i.e., greet him in a friendly manner (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.18.7">Exo 18:7</reference>). The word לחי is obscure, and was interpreted by the early translators merely according to uncertain conjectures. The simplest explanation is apparently <hi type="italic">in vitam</hi>, long <hi type="italic">life</hi>, understood as a wish in the sense of “good fortune to you” (Luther, Maurer, etc.); although the word חי in the singular can only be shown to have the meaning <hi type="italic">life</hi> in connection with the formula used in oaths, נפשׁך חי, etc. But even if חי must be taken as an adjective, it is impossible to explain לחי in any other way than as an elliptical exclamation meaning “good fortune to the living man.” For the idea that the word is to be connected with אמרתּם, “say to the living man,” i.e., to the man if still alive, is overthrown by the fact that David had no doubt that Nabal was still living. The words which follow are also to be understood as a wish, “<hi type="italic">May thou and thy house, and all that is thine, be well!</hi>” After this salutation they were to proceed with the object of their visit: “<hi type="italic">And now I have heard that thou hast sheep-shearers</hi>. <hi type="italic">Now thy shepherds have been with us; we have done them no harm</hi> (הכלים, as in Jdg 18:7 : on the form, see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §53, 3, Anm. 6), <hi type="italic">and nothing was missed by them so long as they were in Carmel</hi>.” When living in the desert, David’s men had associated with the shepherds of Nabal, rendered them various services, and protected them and their flocks against the southern inhabitants of the desert (the Bedouin Arabs); in return for which they may have given them food and information. Thus David proved himself a protector of his people even in his banishment. וימצאוּ, “<hi type="italic">so may the young men</hi> (those sent by David) <hi type="italic">find favour in thine eyes! for we have come to a good</hi> (i.e., a festive) <hi type="italic">day. Give, I pray, what thy hand findeth</hi> (i.e., as much as thou canst) <hi type="italic">to thy servant, and to thy son David</hi>.” With the expression “<hi type="italic">thy son</hi>” David claims Nabal’s fatherly goodwill. So far as the fact itself is concerned, “on such a festive occasion near a town or village even in our own time, an Arab sheikh of the neighbouring desert would hardly fail to put in a word either in person or by message; and his message both in form and substance would be only the transcript of that of David” (<hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, <hi type="italic">Palestine</hi>, p. 201).
entries.262a2d50b3785ffc0f27645fe4aec1c6d0396864: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.9">1Sa 25:9</reference> <div eID="gen4099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4100" type="x-p"/> David’s messengers delivered their message to Nabal, ויּנוּחוּ, “<hi type="italic">and sat down</hi>,” sc., awaiting the fulfilment of their request. The rendering given by the Chaldee (פּסקוּ, <hi type="italic">cessaverunt loqui</hi>) and the Vulgate (<hi type="italic">siluerunt</hi>) is less suitable, and cannot be philologically sustained. The Septuagint, on the other hand, has καὶ ἀνεπήδησε, “and he (Nabal) sprang up,” as if the translators had read ויּקם (vid., lxx at <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.34">1Sa 20:34</reference>). This rendering, according to which the word belongs to the following clause, gives a very appropriate sense, if only, supposing that ויּקם really did stand in the text, the origin and general adoption of ויּנוּחוּ could in any way be explained.
entries.5bd7329a9df68090d11010eef61658ddbc197c6b: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.10">1Sa 25:10</reference> <div eID="gen4100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4101" type="x-p"/> Nabal refused the petitioners in the most churlish manner: “<hi type="italic">Who is David? who the son of Jesse?</hi>” i.e., what have I to do with David? “<hi type="italic">There by many servants now-a-days who tear away every one from his master</hi>.” Thus, in order to justify his own covetousness, he set down David as a vagrant who had run away from his master.
entries.23be0c0f2507947a57cb7e1b3ba04b429a46d11f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.11">1Sa 25:11</reference> <div eID="gen4101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4102" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And I should take my bread and my water (i.e., my food and drink), and my cattle, ... and give them to men whom I do not know whence they are?</hi>” ולקחתּי is a perfect with <hi type="italic">vav consec</hi>., and the whole sentence is to be taken as a question.
entries.184ed3400fe870213ff50d7050c9dc6667731536: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.12-1Sam.25.13">1Sa 25:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen4102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4103" type="x-p"/> The messengers returned to David with this answer. The churlish reply could not fail to excite his anger. He therefore commanded his people to gird on the sword, and started with 400 men to take vengeance upon Nabal, whilst 200 remained behind with the things. 1 Samuel 25:14-31 <div eID="gen4103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4104" type="x-p"/> However intelligible David’s wrath may appear in the situation in which he was placed, it was not right before God, but a sudden burst of sinful passion, which was unseemly in a servant of God. By carrying out his intention, he would have sinned against the Lord and against His people. But the Lord preserved him from this sin by the fact that, just at the right time, Abigail, the intelligent and pious wife of Nabal, heard of the affair, and was able to appease the wrath of David by her immediate and kindly interposition.
entries.66de620a6a381b416da9c76cd20d9c46a1e35ef1: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.14-1Sam.25.16">1Sa 25:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen4104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4105" type="x-p"/> Abigail heard from one of (Nabal’s) servants what had taken place (בּרך, to wish any one prosperity and health, i.e., to salute, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.10">1Sa 13:10</reference>; and יעט, from עיט, to speak wrathfully: on the form, see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.19">1Sa 15:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sa 14:32</reference>), and also what had been praiseworthy in the behaviour of David’s men towards Nabal’s shepherds; how they had not only done them no injury, had not robbed them of anything, but had defended them all the while. “<hi type="italic">They were a wall</hi> (i.e., a firm protection) <hi type="italic">round us by night and by day, as long as we were with them feeding the sheep</hi>,” i.e., a wall of defence against attacks from the Bedouins living in the desert.
entries.9c8eaf38a23c39656fd4f07e2eebe8200ec762ba: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.17">1Sa 25:17</reference> <div eID="gen4105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4106" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And now</hi>,” continued the servant, “<hi type="italic">know and see what thou doest; for evil is determined </hi>(cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.9">1Sa 20:9</reference>) <hi type="italic">against our master and all his house: and he </hi>(Nabal)<hi type="italic">is a wicked man, that one cannot address him</hi>.”
entries.d9bec9f1a3dd711df9d92627452fece80a99e14f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18-1Sam.25.19">1Sa 25:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen4106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4107" type="x-p"/> Then Abigail took as quickly as possible a bountiful present of provisions, - <hi type="italic">two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five prepared</hi> (i.e., slaughtered) <hi type="italic">sheep</hi> (עשׁוּות, a rare form for עשׂוּית: see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §189, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.), <hi type="italic">five seahs</hi> (an ephah and two-thirds) <hi type="italic">of roasted grains</hi> (<hi type="italic">Kali</hi>: see <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.17">1Sa 17:17</reference>), <hi type="italic">a hundred</hi> צמּקים (dried grapes, i.e., raisin-cakes: Ital. <hi type="italic">simmuki</hi>), <hi type="italic">and two hundred fig-cakes</hi> (consisting of pressed figs joined together), - and sent these gifts laden upon asses on before her to meet David whilst she herself followed behind to appease his anger by coming to meet him in a friendly manner, but without saying a word to her husband about what she intended to do.
entries.b8ecc5dca3f965fd850c2a800df76b1707341c20: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.20">1Sa 25:20</reference> <div eID="gen4107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4108" type="x-p"/> When she came down riding upon the ass by a hidden part of the mountain, David and his men came to meet her, so that she lighted upon them. ההר סתר, a hidden part of the mountain, was probably a hollow between two peaks of a mountain. This would explain the use of the word ירד, to come down, with reference both to Abigail, who approached on the one side, and David, who came on the other.
entries.01e3068eed5dc9ccb88b4304562b51ceb23f81ba: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.21-1Sam.25.22">1Sa 25:21-22</reference> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.21">1Sa 25:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.22">1Sa 25:22</reference> contain a circumstantial clause introduced parenthetically to explain what follows: but David had said, <hi type="italic">Only for deception</hi> (i.e., for no other purpose than to be deceived in my expectation) <hi type="italic">have I defended all that belongs to this man</hi> (Nabal) <hi type="italic">in the desert, so that nothing of his was missed, and</hi> (for) <hi type="italic">he hath repaid me evil for good. God do so to the enemies of David, if I leave</hi>, etc.; i.e., “as truly as God will punish the enemies of David, so certainly will I not leave till the morning light, of all that belongeth to him, one that pisseth against the wall.” This oath, in which the punishment of God is not called down upon the swearer himself (God do so <hi type="italic">to me</hi>), as it generally is, but upon the enemies of David, is analogous to that in <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.17">1Sa 3:17</reference>, where punishment is threatened upon the person addressed, who is there made to swear; except that here, as the oath could not be uttered in the ears of the person addressed, upon whom it was to fall, the enemies generally are mentioned instead of “<hi type="italic">to thee</hi>.” There is no doubt, therefore, as to the correctness of the text. The substance of this imprecation may be explained from the fact that David is so full of the consciousness of fighting and suffering for the cause of the kingdom of God, that he discerns in the insult heaped upon him by Nabal an act of hostility to the Lord and the cause of His kingdom. The phrase בּקיר משׁתּין, <hi type="italic">mingens in parietem</hi>, is only met with in passages which speak of the destruction of a family or household to the very last man (viz., besides this passage, 1Ki 14:10; 1Ki 16:11; 1Ki 21:21; 2Ki 9:8), and neither refers primarily to dogs, as Ephraem Syrus, Juda ben Karish, and others maintain; nor to the lowest class of men, as Winer, Maurer, and others imagine; nor to little boys, as L. de Dieu, <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>, etc., suppose; but, as we may see from the explanatory clause appended to 1Ki 14:10; 1Ki 21:21; 2Ki 9:8, to every male (<hi type="italic">quemcumque masculi generis hominem:</hi> vid., Bochart, <hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. i. pp. 776ff., and Rödiger on <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. pp. 1397-8).
entries.039d9ad12a042b959df5ee7bda40609f6540c247: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.23-1Sam.25.24">1Sa 25:23-24</reference> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.23">1Sa 25:23</reference> is connected with 1Sa 25:20. When Abigail saw David, she descended hastily from the ass, fell upon her face before him, bowed to the ground, and fell at his feet, saying, “<hi type="italic">Upon me, me, my lord, be the guilt; allow thy handmaid to reveal the thing to thee</hi>.” She takes the guilt upon herself, because she hopes that David will not avenge it upon her.
entries.1b1a43ee72b13edca3336866f59ac5e971fef1cf: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.25-1Sam.25.26">1Sa 25:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen4108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4109" type="x-p"/> She prayed that David would take no notice of Nabal, for he was what his name declared - <hi type="italic">a fool, and folly in him</hi>; but she (Abigail) had not seen the messengers of David. “The prudent woman uses a good argument; for a wise man should pardon a fool” (Seb. Schmidt). She then endeavours to bring David to a friendly state of mind by three arguments, introduced with ועתּה (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.26">1Sa 25:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.27">1Sa 25:27</reference>), before asking for forgiveness (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.28">1Sa 25:28</reference>). She first of all pointed to the leadings of God, by which David had been kept from committing murder through her coming to meet him.<note placement="foot">“She founds her argument upon their meeting, which was so marvellously seasonable, that it might be easily and truly gathered from this fact that it had taken place through the providence of God; i.e., And now, because I meet thee so seasonably, do thou piously acknowledge with me the providence of God, which has so arranged all this, that innocent blood might not by change be shed by thee.” - <hi type="italic">Seb. Schmidt</hi>.</note> “As <hi type="italic">truly as Jehovah liveth, and by the life of thy soul! yea, the Lord hath kept thee, that thou camest not into blood-guiltiness, and thy hand helped thee</hi>” (i.e., and with thy hand thou didst procure thyself help). אשׁר, introducing her words, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.20">1Sa 15:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “as truly as thou livest, (so true is it) that,” etc. In the second place, she points to the fact that God is the avenger of the wicked, by expressing the wish that all the enemies of David may become fools like Nabal; in connection with which it must be observed, in order to understand her words fully, that, according to the Old Testament representation, folly is a correlate of ungodliness, which inevitably brings down punishment.<note placement="foot">Seb. Schmidt has justly observed, that “she reminds David of the promise of God. Not that she prophesies, but that she has gathered it from the general promises of the word of God. The promise referred to is, that whoever does good to his enemies, and takes no vengeance upon them, God himself will avenge him upon his enemies; according to the saying, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine, I will repay</hi>. And this is what Abigail says: And now thine enemies shall be as Nabal.”</note> <div eID="gen4109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4110" type="x-p"/> The predicate to the sentence “<hi type="italic">and they that seek evil to my lord</hi>” must be supplied from the preceding words, viz., “<hi type="italic">may they become just such fools</hi>.”
entries.ff48ce06d809ef6ef62ee6affcef77d1cd2690db: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.27">1Sa 25:27</reference> <div eID="gen4110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4111" type="x-p"/> It is only in the third line that she finally mentions the present, but in such a manner that she does not offer it directly to David, but describes it as a gift for the men in his train. “<hi type="italic">And now this blessing</hi> (בּרכה here and <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.26">1Sa 30:26</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.33.11">Gen 33:11</reference> : cf. ἡ εὐλογία, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.5-2Cor.9.6">2Co 9:5-6</reference>), <hi type="italic">which thine handmaid hath brought, let it be given to the young men in my lord’s train</hi>” (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “at the feet of:” cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.11.8">Exo 11:8</reference>; Jdg 4:10, etc.).
entries.67bcc60993f16561ffc9791d05111131eae9aad4: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.28">1Sa 25:28</reference> <div eID="gen4111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4112" type="x-p"/> The shrewd and pious woman supports her prayer for forgiveness of the wrong, which she takes upon herself, by promises of the rich blessing with which the Lord would recompense David. She thereby gives such clear and distinct expression to her firm belief in the divine election of David as king of Israel, that her words almost amount to prophecy: “<hi type="italic">For Jehovah will make my lord a lasting house</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.35">1Sa 2:35</reference>; and for the fact itself, 2Sa 7:8., where the Lord confirms this pious wish by His own promises to David himself); <hi type="italic">for my lord fighteth the wars of Jehovah</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17">1Sa 18:17</reference>), <hi type="italic">and evil is not discovered in thee thy whole life long</hi>.” רעה, evil, i.e., misfortune, mischief; for the thought that he might also be preserved from wrong-doing is not expressed till 1Sa 25:31. “<hi type="italic">All thy days</hi>,” <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “from thy days,” i.e., from the beginning of thy life.
entries.01c5a77c97068a77d7803e994d68dfda68823adf: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1Sa 25:29</reference> <div eID="gen4112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4113" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And should any one rise up to pursue thee, ... the soul of my lord will be bound up in the bundle of the living with the Lord thy God</hi>.” The metaphor is taken from the custom of binding up valuable things in a bundle, to prevent their being injured. The words do not refer primarily to eternal life with God in heaven, but only to the safe preservation of the righteous on this earth in the grace and fellowship of the Lord. But whoever is so hidden in the gracious fellowship of the Lord in this life, that no enemy can harm him or injure his life, the Lord will not allow to perish, even though temporal death should come, but will then receive him into eternal life. “But the soul of thine enemies, He will hurl away in the cup of the sling.” “The cup (caph: cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Gen 32:26</reference>) of the sling” was the cavity in which the stone was placed for the purpose of hurling.
entries.b50e5e909aaf016409494616a59420f68eea360d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.30-1Sam.25.31">1Sa 25:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen4113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4114" type="x-p"/> Abigail concluded her intercession with the assurance that the forgiveness of Nabal’s act would be no occasion of anguish of heart to David when he should have become prince over Israel, on account of his having shed innocent blood and helped himself, and also with the hope that he would remember her. From the words, “<hi type="italic">When Jehovah shall do to my lord according to all the good that He hath spoken concerning him, and shall make thee prince over Israel</hi>,” it appears to follow that Abigail had received certain information of the anointing of David, and his designation to be the future king, probably through Samuel, or one of the pupils of the prophets. There is nothing to preclude this assumption, even if it cannot be historically sustained. Abigail manifests such an advance and maturity in the life of faith, as could only have been derived from intercourse with prophets. It is expressly stated with regard to Elijah and Elisha, that at certain times the pious assembled together around the prophets. What prevents us from assuming the same with regard to Samuel? The absence of any distinct testimony to that effect is amply compensated for by the brief, and for the most part casual, notices that are given of the influence which Samuel exerted upon all Israel.
entries.9beb631b1d9d668a637effec7f0fb8c682a4d86d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.32-1Sam.25.34">1Sa 25:32-34</reference> <div eID="gen4114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4115" type="x-p"/> These words could not fail to appease David’s wrath. In his reply he praised the Lord for having sent Abigail to meet him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.32">1Sa 25:32</reference>), and then congratulated Abigail upon her understanding and her actions, that she had kept him from bloodshed (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.33">1Sa 25:33</reference>); otherwise he would certainly have carried out the revenge which he had resolved to take upon Nabal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.34">1Sa 25:34</reference>). ואוּלם is strongly adversative: <hi type="italic">nevertheless</hi>. מהרע, <hi type="italic">inf. constr. Hiph</hi>. of רעע. כּי, ὅτι, introduces the substance of the affirmation, and is repeated before the oath: אם כּי ... לוּלי כּי, (that) <hi type="italic">if thou hadst not</hi>, etc., (that) <hi type="italic">truly there would not have been left</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.27">2Sa 2:27</reference>). The very unusual form תּבאתי, an imperfect with the termination of the perfect, might indeed possibly be a copyist’s error for תּבאי (Olsh. <hi type="italic">Gr</hi>. pp. 452, 525), but in all probability it is only an intensified form of the second pers. fem. imperf., like תּבואתה (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.16">Deu 33:16</reference>; cf. <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §191, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.).
entries.f1277f4c2e69faba2dddc5388042d4851f2a648a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.35">1Sa 25:35</reference> <div eID="gen4115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4116" type="x-p"/> David then received the gifts brought for him, and bade Abigail return to her house, with the assurance that he had granted her request for pardon. פּנים נשׂא, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.21">Gen 19:21</reference>, etc.
entries.eec810712be2048cf829391d1a02310e4b692261: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36">1Sa 25:36</reference> <div eID="gen4116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4117" type="x-p"/> When Abigail returned home, she found her husband <hi type="italic">at a great feast, like a king’s feast, very merry</hi> (עליו, “therewith,” refers to משׁתּה: cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.30">Pro 23:30</reference>), <hi type="italic">and drunken above measure</hi>, so that she told him nothing of what had occurred until the break of day.
entries.0fd9fb20651d6f6fa9fad9cd5d7505fa8a94256e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.37">1Sa 25:37</reference> <div eID="gen4117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4118" type="x-p"/> Then, “<hi type="italic">when the wine had gone from Nabal</hi>,” i.e., when he had become sober, she related the matter to him; whereat he was so terrified, that he was smitten with a stroke. This is the meaning of the words, “<hi type="italic">his heart died within him, and it became as stone</hi>.” The cause of it was not his anger at the loss he had sustained, or merely his alarm at the danger to which he had been exposed, and which he did not believe to be over yet, but also his vexation that his wife should have made him humble himself in such a manner; for he is described as a hard, i.e., an unbending, self-willed man.
entries.e91e68f5c871041511fb9b92678a69347f56e9a2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.38">1Sa 25:38</reference> <div eID="gen4118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4119" type="x-p"/> About ten days later <hi type="italic">the Lord smote him so that he died</hi>, i.e., the Lord put an end to his life by a second stroke.
entries.4a6697d1bcf4c076110bba01e1e4d18a370e3c0b: <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.39-1Sam.25.44">1Sa 25:39-44</reference> <div eID="gen4119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4120" type="x-p"/> When David heard of Nabal’s death, he praised Jehovah that He had avenged his shame upon Nabal, and held him back from self-revenge. וגו רב עשׁר, “<hi type="italic">who hath pleaded the cause of my reproach</hi> (the disgrace inflicted upon me) <hi type="italic">against Nabal</hi>.” “<hi type="italic">Against Nabal</hi>” does not belong to “<hi type="italic">my reproach</hi>,” but to “<hi type="italic">pleaded the cause</hi>.” The construction of ריב with מן is a pregnant one, to fight (and deliver) out of the power of a person (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1">Psa 43:1</reference>); whereas here the fundamental idea is that of taking vengeance upon a person.

                  <ns0:p n="14">14 ¶ But one of the young men told Abigail <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Wisely considering the mischievous effects likely to fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low so churlish a message.</ns0:note> Nabals wife, saying, Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master; and he <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> flew upon them.</ns0:note> railed on them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 But the men <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> very good unto us and we were not <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> shamed.</ns0:note> hurt, neither missed we any thing as long as we were conversant with them, when we were in the fields.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 They were a wall <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A defence against wild Beasts, and Robbers, and Enemies.</ns0:note> unto us both by night and day, all the while we were with them keep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the sheep.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 Now therefore know, and consider what thou wilt do: for evil is determined against our master, and against all his houshold <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which it was easie to guess; either, from some threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning expressions which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s men used; or, from the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sideration of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s great power, and that rage which so high a provocation was likely to produce in Military Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons.</ns0:note>: for he <ns0:hi>is such</ns0:hi> a son of Belial, that <ns0:hi>a man</ns0:hi> cannot speak to him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To wit, without hazard to himself, and therefore I acquaint thee, rather than him, with this matter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 ¶ Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which she did without his leave, and against his mind, because it was a case of apparent necessity, for the preserva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of her self, and Husband, and all the Family from im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minent ruin. And surely that real and urgent necessity which dispenseth with Gods positive commands, might well dispense with the Husbands right, in this case.</ns0:note>, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> clusters of rai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> on asses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And she said unto her servants, Go on before me, behold, I come after you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For she knew she could quickly overtake them.</ns0:note>: but she told not her husband Nabal.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And it was <ns0:hi>so, as</ns0:hi> she rode on the asse, that she came down by the covert of the hill <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In the lower part, and under the shadow of the Hill, or of the Trees that grew upon it; so that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did not see her till she met him.</ns0:note>, and behold, David and his men came down <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, from another opposite Hill.</ns0:note> against her, and she met them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 (Now David had said <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either in his journey, or as soon as he heard that re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proachful answer.</ns0:note>, Surely in vain have I kept all that this <ns0:hi>fellow</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Whom he thought unworthy to be named, for his barbarous ingratitude and churlishness.</ns0:note> hath in the wilder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, so that nothing was missed of all that <ns0:hi>per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tained</ns0:hi> unto him, and he hath requited me evil for good.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 So, and more also do God unto the enemies of David <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Unto <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> himself. But because it might seem ominous and unnatural to Curse himself, therefore by a Fi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gure called <ns0:hi>Euphemismus,</ns0:hi> instead of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> he mentions <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Enemies.</ns0:hi> See 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 16. The words may be thus rendred: <ns0:hi>So and more also let God do: for</ns0:hi> (the Hebrew <ns0:hi>La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med</ns0:hi> being very oft so used) <ns0:hi>the Enemies of David,</ns0:hi> i. e. Let God work for them, and give them as much Prosperity and Success as <ns0:hi>Nabal</ns0:hi> hath hitherto had. Or, let God utter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly destroy their Enemies; and especially, my self the chief of them, if I do not destroy this man.</ns0:note>, if I leave of all that <ns0:hi>pertain</ns0:hi> unto him by the morning light, any that pisseth against the wall <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Any of the Males, for they onely do so; and of them this Phrase is manifestly understood; 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 14. 10. and 21. 21. and 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 9. 8. And men not wholly barbarous have generally spared Women in such cases. <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> Why then was <ns0:hi>Abigail</ns0:hi> so much concer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned and afraid? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Partly from humanity, and the hor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ror of so general and dreadful a Slaughter of her Family and nearest Relations: and partly, because when the Sword was once drawn, she knew not where it would rest, nor whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther she should escape: for she knew nothing of this limita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s threatning, till she came to him.</ns0:note>).</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:241" />23 And when Abigail saw David, she hasted and lighted off the ass, and fell before David on her face, and bowed her self to the ground <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Not onely in token of deep reverence, but as a most humble suppliant; as 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 4. 27.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And fell at his feet, and said, Upon me, my LORD, <ns0:hi>upon</ns0:hi> me let <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> iniquity <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Impute <ns0:hi>Nabal</ns0:hi>'s Sin to me, and, if thou pleasest, punish it in me, who here offer my self as a Sacrifice to thy just In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dignation. This whole Speech of <ns0:hi>Abigail</ns0:hi> is done with great artifice; and she doth here, by an absolute submitting to Mercy, without any pretence of justification of what was done, but rather with aggravation of it) indeavour to work upon <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s generosity, and good nature, to pardon it. And, with great art, first would divert the punishment from her Hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />band to her self, because she had then much more to say, why <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> should spare her, then why he should spare <ns0:hi>Nabal.</ns0:hi> And there was hardly any need of Argument, whence the greatest Orator might argue in this case, which she doth not manage to the best advantage, and most plausible insinuations for such an exigent.</ns0:note>, and let thine handmaid, I pray thee, speak in thine <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> ear.</ns0:note> audience, and hear the words of thine handmaid.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 Let not my lord, I pray thee, † regard <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">His Person and Words deserve thy contempt, but not thy regard.</ns0:note> this<ns0:note place="margin">‡ <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> lay <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to his heart.</ns0:note> man of Belial <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For such he hath shewed himself to be by this wicked and abominable carriage towards thee.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> Nabal: for as his name <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he: Nabal <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> his name, and folly <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with him <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">His noted folly and stupidity is a more proper Object for thy pity than anger. His fordid Answer to thy Servants did not proceed from any ill design, or deep malice, but from bru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tish So<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>tishness, and want of the understanding of a man in him. It may be thought a great Crime, that she traduceth her Husband in this manner. But this may be said for her, That she told them nothing but what they all knew con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning him, and that she onely seemed to take away that which he never had indeed, to wit, his good name, that she might preserve that which he had, and which was more dear and important to him, even his Life and Soul.</ns0:note>: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Though I freely submit my self to the Punishment in my Husbands stead, yet I was innocent of the Crime.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 Now therefore, my lord, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the LORD liveth, and <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> thy soul liveth, seeing the LORD hath with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />holden thee from coming to <ns0:hi>shed</ns0:hi> blood <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Seeing God hath so ordered this business by his wise and wonderful Providence, that I should accidentally, and unex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pectedly come to the knowledge of my Husbands vile and sordid Carriage; and that I should come to meet thee, and find thee so gracious, as to give me a favourable Audience; and all this, that hereby he might with-hold thee from the Sin of Blood-guiltiness,</ns0:note>, and from <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> saving thy self.</ns0:note> avenging thy self with thine own hand: now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord be as Nabal <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Let them be as contemptible and hateful as <ns0:hi>Nabal</ns0:hi> is, and will be for this odious Action; let them be as unable to do thee any hurt as he is; let them be forced to yeild to thee, and implore thy Pardon and Favour, as <ns0:hi>Nabal</ns0:hi> now doth by my mouth: let the Vengeance thou didst design upon <ns0:hi>Nabal</ns0:hi> and his Family, fall upon their heads, who by their constant and inveterate Malice against thee, do more deserve it than this silly Fool for this one mis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />carriage; and much more than all the rest of our Family, who as they are none of thine Enemies, nor such as seek thee evil, so they were no way guilty of this wicked Action. And therefore spare these, and execute thy Vengeance up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on more proper Objects.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And now this <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> present.</ns0:note> blessing <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">So a gift or present is called here, and <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 33. 11. and elsewhere; not onely because the matter of it comes from Gods blessing; but also because it is given with a Ble<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ing, or with a good will.</ns0:note> which thine hand maid hath brought unto my lord, let it even be given unto the young men that <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> walk at the feet or <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> follow my lord <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">As being unworthy of thine accep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance or use.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 I pray thee, forgive the trespass of thine hand-maid <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Which I have taken upon my self, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24. and which, if it be not Pardoned, but Punished, the Punishment will reach to me.</ns0:note>: for the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Will give the Kingdom to thee, and to thy House for ever, as he hath promised thee. And there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore let Gods great kindness to thee, make thee gentle and merciful to others; do not fully thy approaching Glory with the stain of Innocent Blood; but consider, that it is the glory of a King (which thou art by Gods appointment, and shall ere long actually be) to pass by Offences; and that it will be thy loss to cut off such as will shortly be thy Sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects.</ns0:note>, because my lord fighteth the battels of the LORD <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> For the Lord, and for the People of the Lord against their Enemies; especially, the <ns0:hi>Philistines.</ns0:hi> And as that is thy proper Work, and therein thou mayest expect Gods blessing and help; so it is not thy work to draw thy Sword in thy own private quarrel against any of the people of the Lord; and God will not bless thee in it.</ns0:note>, and evil hath not been found in thee, <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> thy days <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Though thou hast been oft aspersed, and charged with many Crimes, by <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and others; yet thy Innocency hath been, and is evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent to all men: do not therefore now by this cruel act of Vengeance justifie thine Enemies Reproaches, nor blemish thy great and just Reputation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Yet a man <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> though no way injured nor justly provoked by thee.</ns0:note> is risen to pursue thee, and to seek thy soul <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To take away thy Life.</ns0:note>: but the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in the bun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dle: i. e.</ns0:hi> In the Society, or Congregation <ns0:hi>of the living;</ns0:hi> out of which, men are taken, and cut off by Death. The Phrase is taken from the common usage of men, who bind those things in bundles, which they are afraid to lose, because things that are solitary and unbound, are soon lost. The meaning of the place is, God will preserve thy Life; and therefore it becomes not thee, unjustly and unnecessarily to take away the Lives of any; especially, of the People of thy God and Saviour.</ns0:note> with the LORD thy God <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the hand and custody of God, who by his watchful Providence, preserves this<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Bun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dle, and all that are in it; and thee in a particular and singular manner, as being <ns0:hi>thy God</ns0:hi> in a peculiar way, and special Covenant. God himself will hide, and keep thee in the secret of his Presence. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 31. 20. where no hand of violence can reach thee. And therefore all the Attempts of <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> or others against thee, are vain and ridiculous. For who can Destroy whom God will keep?</ns0:note>, and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in the midst of the bought of a sling.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>as out</ns0:hi> of the middle of a sling <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">God himself will cut them off suddenly, violently, and irresistibly; and cast them far away, both from his Presence, and from thy Neighbourhood, and from all capacity of doing thee any hurt.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And it shall come to pass, when the LORD shall have done to my lord, according to all the good that he hath spoken concerning thee, and shall have appointed thee ruler over Israel;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 That this shall be <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> no stag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gering <ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> stumbling.</ns0:note> no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Thy Mind and Conscience will be free from all the Tor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment which the guilt and shame of such an Action would cause in thee. By which, she cunningly <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nsinuates, what a Blemish this would be to his Glory, what a disturbance to his Peace and Felicity, if he proceeded to execute his Pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose: and withal implies, how sweet and comfortable it would be to him to remember, that he had for conscience to God denied himself, and restrained his Passions.</ns0:note>, either that thou hast shed blood causless <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which she signifies would be done if he should go on. For though <ns0:hi>Nabal</ns0:hi> had been guilty of abominable Rudeness, Uncharita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bleness, and Ingratitude; yet he had done nothing worthy of Death, by the Laws of God or of Man. And whatsoever he had done, the rest of his Family were innocent.</ns0:note>, or that my lord <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> saved himself, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 26.</ns0:note> hath avenged himself <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Which is directly contrary to Gods Law, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 19. 18. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 35. compare with <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12. 19.</ns0:note>: but when the LORD shall have dealt well with my lord, then remember thine handmaid <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">When God shall make thee King, and I shall have occasion to apply my self to thee for Justice, or Relief, let me find Grace in thy sight, and so let me do at this time. Or, <ns0:hi>and the Lord will bless my lord,</ns0:hi> and recompence thee for this Mortification of thy Passion, and <ns0:hi>thou wilt remember thine handmaid: i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou wiltst remember my Counsel with satisfaction to thy self, and thankfulness to me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:242" />32 ¶ And David said unto Abigail, Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which by his gracious and singular Providence so dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed Matters, that thou shouldest come to me: He rightly begins at the Fountain of this Deliverance, which was God; and then proceeds to the Instruments.</ns0:note> this day to meet me:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> thy advice, and blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> thou <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Lord bless and recompence thee, for this thy good Advice.</ns0:note>, which hast kept me this day from coming to <ns0:hi>shed</ns0:hi> blood <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which I had sworn to do. Hereby it plain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly appears, That Oaths whereby men bind themselves to any Sin, are Null and Void: and as it was a Sin to make them; so it is adding sin to sin to perform them.</ns0:note>, and from avenging my self with mine own hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 For in very deed, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the Lord God of Israel liveth, which hath kept me back from hurting thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not that he intended to Kill her, but the Males onely; as was noted on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. But their Destruction, was a dread<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Affliction and Damage to her.</ns0:note>, except thou hadst hasted and come to meet me, surely there had not been left unto Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bal by the morning light, any that pisseth against the wall.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 So David received of her hand <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> which she had brought him, and said unto her, Go up in peace to thine house: see, I have hearkened to thy voice, and have accepted thy person <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Shewed my Acceptance of thy Person, by my grant of thy Request: See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 19. 21,</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 ¶ And Abigail came to Nabal, and behold he held a feast in his house like the feast of a king <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">As the manner was upon those Solemn Occasions. Sor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />did Covetousness, and vain Prodigality were met together in him.</ns0:note>, and Nabals heart <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> merry within him, for he <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> very drunken: wherefore she told him no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He being then uncapable of Admonition, his Rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son and Conscience being both asleep.</ns0:note>, less or more, until the morning light.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 But it came to pass in the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, and his wife had told him these things, that his hea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t died within him, and he became <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> a stone <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He was oppressed with Grief, and fainted away through the fear and horror of so great a Mischief, though it was past. As one, who having in the Night galloped over a nar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />row Plank, laid upon a broken Bridge, over a steep River; when in the Morning he came to review it, was struck Dead with the horror of the danger he was in.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 And it came to pass about ten days <ns0:hi>after,</ns0:hi> that the LORD smote Naba<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, that he died <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">God either inflicted some other stroke or Disease upon him, or increased his Grief and Fear to such an height, as killed him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 ¶ And when David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the LORD, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">How could <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> rejoyce at the Death of his Enemy? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Although it may be said, that he rejoyced not in <ns0:hi>Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bal's</ns0:hi> Death as such, but onely in the declaration of Gods Justice in Punishing so great a Wickedness; which was an honour to God, and a document, and therefore a benefit to Mankind, and so a Publick good, and cause of Joy: yet the matter is not weighty, if we confess, that this was another instance of Humane Infirmity iu <ns0:hi>Duvid,</ns0:hi> and that it is not proposed for our Imitation, but for our Caution. Yet it may be further said, That this was not purely an act of Private Revenge, because <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was a Publick Person, and Anoin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted King: and therefore <ns0:hi>Nabal's</ns0:hi> Reproach cast upon <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> above, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10, 11. was a Contempt of God, and of his Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinance, and Appointment; which was vindicated by this remarkable Judgment.</ns0:note>, and hath kept his servant from evil <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From the Sin of Bloodshed, and Self-revenge, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 33.</ns0:note>: for the LORD hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. And David sent <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To wit, Messengers; which he thought fitter than to go himself: partly, because if he had met with a Repulse, it had been less Ignominions; and partly, because he would leave her to her freedom and choice, and would not so much as seem to take her by vio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lence. But this doubtless was not done immediately after <ns0:hi>Nabal's</ns0:hi> Death, but in some convenient space of time after it; though such Circumstances be commonly omitted in the Sacred History; which gives onely the Heads, and most Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portant Passages of things.</ns0:note> and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40 And when the setvants of David were come to Abigail to Carmel, they spake unto her, saying, David sent us unto thee, to take thee to him to wife.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="41">41 And she arose, and bowed her self on <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> face to the earth, and said <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">She shewed this Reverence, and spake thus to them, as representing <ns0:hi>David's</ns0:hi> person.</ns0:note>, Behold, <ns0:hi>let</ns0:hi> thine hand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />maid <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.</ns0:p>
